G01-T01.open: Hey — good to see you. You've opened NULL Check, the very first lesson in Completeness, so let's lock in the foundation everything else builds on. Three quick checks, and I'll tell you exactly what you nailed and what to watch for as we go.

questions.q: Why does `WHERE Email = NULL` return zero rows, even for records where Email actually is NULL?
choices: '=' comparisons against NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so the row is never matched
SQL Server silently converts NULL to an empty string before comparing
Email is a reserved word and can't be compared directly
The query needs a GROUP BY before NULL can be evaluated
questions.right: Exactly right — and that's the whole lesson in one sentence. NULL isn't a value you can compare against, it's the absence of one, so '=' can never touch it. You've got the core idea. Onto the next one.
questions.wrong: Not quite, but you're close enough that this will click fast. Here's the key: NULL isn't a value — it's the absence of one. So '=' can't compare against it any more than it can compare against nothing at all. Every '=' test against NULL comes back UNKNOWN, not TRUE, which is why the row silently disappears from your results.

questions.q: In the field-level summary query, why does the lesson use UNION ALL instead of plain UNION?
choices: UNION ALL keeps every row, including ones that look identical, instead of silently deduplicating them
UNION ALL runs faster because it sorts the columns first
Plain UNION cannot combine three SELECT statements, only two
UNION ALL is required whenever COUNT(*) appears in a SELECT
questions.right: Yes — good instinct there. UNION quietly merges rows that look identical across every column, and if two fields happened to land on the same count and percentage, you'd lose one silently. UNION ALL protects you from that.
questions.wrong: Good try, but here's the trap this question is testing for: plain UNION removes rows that are exact duplicates across every column. If two different fields happened to have the same NullCount and NullPct, UNION would silently merge them into one row and you'd lose a field from your report without any error. UNION ALL guarantees every field keeps its own line.

questions.q: Why does the query write `COUNT(*) * 100.0` instead of `COUNT(*) * 100`?
choices: Without the .0, SQL Server performs integer division and the percentage truncates to 0%
The .0 tells SQL Server to round to the nearest whole number
It has no effect — both produce identical results
The .0 is required syntax whenever COUNT(*) is divided by anything
questions.right: You caught the integer-division trap — that one bites a lot of people the first time they see it. Multiplying by a bare integer keeps everything in integer math, and a real percentage like 10% would round straight down to 0.
questions.wrong: This one's sneaky, so no worries — here's what's actually happening. Multiplying by the plain integer 100 keeps the whole expression in integer arithmetic. A genuine result like 2/20 would truncate to 0 before the percentage even gets calculated. Adding .0 forces SQL Server into decimal math, so the real percentage survives instead of silently becoming 0%.

G01-T01.close: Solid session — you've got IS NULL vs '=', UNION ALL vs UNION, and the integer-division trap all locked in. Those three ideas alone will save you from three of the most common SQL Server mistakes people make. Ready for Blank / Empty String next, or want to go deeper here first?

G01-T02.open: Welcome back — this lesson picks up right where NULL Check left off: your NULL check just passed, but emails are still bouncing. Let's find out why together.

questions.q: A migration passes every NULL check, but customers still report bounced emails. What's the most likely cause?
choices: The source system wrote empty strings ('') for missing emails instead of NULL, and IS NULL doesn't catch those
The Email column has the wrong data type
NULL checks only work on numeric columns, not text columns
The migration ran on a weekend, when validation is skipped
questions.right: Exactly — and this is the whole reason G01-T02 exists as its own lesson. A blank string is a real, populated value that just happens to be empty. NULL and blank are two completely different problems that look identical to a customer.
questions.wrong: Close, but the actual answer is more subtle and worth sitting with: a blank string '' is a real, populated value — it's not the same thing as NULL. IS NULL will never catch it, and = '' will never catch a genuine NULL. Your migration script needs to check for both.

questions.q: Why does the query wrap the empty-string check as `LTRIM(RTRIM(Email)) = ''` instead of just `Email = ''`?
choices: So a value like three spaces ('   '), which isn't literally an empty string, is still caught as effectively blank
Because SQL Server requires LTRIM/RTRIM before any string comparison
To make the query run faster by reducing the string length
LTRIM/RTRIM converts the value to uppercase for comparison
questions.right: Right — you're thinking like a data validator now. '   ' isn't literally '' by a strict comparison, but it's just as meaningless. Trimming first catches both cases with one check instead of two.
questions.wrong: Here's the nuance this one's testing: a field containing '   ' (spaces) is not literally equal to '' — a strict comparison would miss it. But it's functionally just as empty. Trimming the value first collapses both cases into one check, so you don't need two separate rules.

questions.q: In `LTRIM(RTRIM(ISNULL(Email, '')))`, why does ISNULL need to run before LTRIM?
choices: Calling LTRIM on a real NULL returns NULL, and `NULL = ''` evaluates to UNKNOWN — silently dropping the row from the results
ISNULL makes the query run in a different execution order for performance
Without ISNULL, LTRIM would throw a syntax error
ISNULL converts the column to a different data type required by LTRIM
questions.right: Nailed it. This is the same UNKNOWN-vs-TRUE trap from the NULL Check lesson showing up again, one layer deeper — LTRIM(NULL) is NULL, and NULL never equals anything, including ''.
questions.wrong: This connects straight back to lesson one, so let's make the link explicit: LTRIM(NULL) returns NULL, not ''. And NULL = '' evaluates to UNKNOWN, the same way NULL = NULL does — so a genuinely-NULL row would silently disappear from your results without ISNULL converting it to '' first.

G01-T02.close: You've now separated two failure modes that look identical from the outside — NULL and blank — and you know exactly how to catch both together. That distinction alone will save real debugging time later. Onto Placeholder Text when you're ready.

G01-T03.open: Alright — this one's about the sneakiest category yet: values that LOOK real but actually mean "we don't know." Let's see how sharp your eye is for spotting them.

questions.q: Why does the placeholder-detection query wrap every comparison in UPPER() before checking against the blocklist?
choices: So 'N/A', 'n/a', and 'N/a' are all caught by one entry in the list, instead of needing every case variant listed separately
UPPER() is required syntax whenever IN() is used in SQL Server
It converts the placeholder text into a numeric code for faster comparison
Lowercase values are always treated as NULL by SQL Server by default
questions.right: Exactly right — one normalized list instead of an endless list of case variants. That's the kind of thing that keeps a validation blocklist maintainable long-term.
questions.wrong: Good instinct to think about the blocklist itself — here's the reasoning: people and systems type placeholder text in every case imaginable. Normalizing everything to UPPER() first means one list entry ('N/A') catches every capitalization, instead of the list growing forever to cover 'n/a', 'N/a', and so on.

questions.q: Why is a DOB of 01/01/1900 treated as suspicious rather than a legitimate birth date?
choices: It's the most common date-field placeholder in legacy systems, historically used as a default "empty" date
SQL Server doesn't allow dates before 1900 to be stored
It's always a data entry typo for the current year
01/01/1900 is a reserved system date that triggers an error
questions.right: Yes — you've spotted the classic sentinel date. That one shows up constantly across legacy systems because it's often the default minimum date value baked into older tools.
questions.wrong: This is worth remembering because you'll see it again and again in real data: 01/01/1900 is the most common "empty date" default in legacy tools — many systems fall back to it when no real date was ever entered. A living customer with that birth date is a strong tell that the value is a placeholder, not a fact.

questions.q: What is the purpose of checking `Phone LIKE '000%'`, `'999%'`, and `'111%'`?
choices: To catch common fake/placeholder phone numbers like all-zeros or all-repeated-digits without listing every possible variant
To find phone numbers from a specific country code
To detect phone numbers that are too short to be valid
To identify numbers that have already been called before
questions.right: Right — you're pattern-matching the way real placeholder data actually shows up. All-zero and all-repeated-digit numbers are the classic "I need to submit this form" fake entries.
questions.wrong: Here's the pattern behind it: numbers like 0000000000 or 9999999999 are the classic entries people type when a form demands a phone number they don't want to give. The LIKE patterns catch these common fake families efficiently, without needing to list every possible fake number by hand.

G01-T03.close: Great pattern-recognition work — you're now catching placeholder values that pass every basic completeness check but are quietly meaningless. This is exactly the kind of thing that separates a careful analyst from one who just runs the obvious query. Ready for Whitespace-Only next?

G01-T04.open: This lesson is a personal favorite of mine to teach because the bug is so invisible — a field that LOOKS populated but is actually just... spaces. Let's dig in.

questions.q: A FirstName field contains three spaces ('   '). Why does `LEN(FirstName)` fail to reveal that it's effectively empty?
choices: LEN() counts every character including spaces, so it returns 3 — the field only looks empty after trimming
LEN() ignores spaces entirely and would return 0 automatically
LEN() only works on numeric columns
Spaces are counted as NULL by SQL Server's LEN function
questions.right: Exactly — LEN() is honest about character count, which is exactly the problem. Three spaces really are three characters. You have to trim first to see the truth underneath.
questions.wrong: This is the whole twist of the lesson, so let's make it click: LEN('   ') genuinely returns 3 — there ARE three characters there, they're just meaningless ones. The field only reveals itself as empty once you trim the spaces away first and measure what's left.

questions.q: Why does the lesson add a separate "deep check" using REPLACE for tabs and carriage returns?
choices: LTRIM and RTRIM only strip space characters — they do not remove tabs (CHAR(9)) or carriage returns (CHAR(13))
REPLACE runs faster than LTRIM/RTRIM on large tables
Tabs and carriage returns are illegal characters that must be removed before any query runs
It's only needed for columns imported from Excel, never from CSV
questions.right: You've got it — LTRIM/RTRIM are more limited than most people assume. They only touch ASCII space, so a tab-only or CR-only field would sail right past them undetected.
questions.wrong: Here's the gap this catches: LTRIM and RTRIM only strip actual space characters — nothing else. A field that's secretly just a tab (CHAR(9)) or a carriage return (CHAR(13)) would pass a plain LTRIM/RTRIM check as "non-empty," because those functions never touch it. REPLACE strips those too before the real emptiness test runs.

questions.q: In `LEN(LTRIM(RTRIM(ISNULL(FirstName, ''))))`, what breaks if ISNULL is left out for a row where FirstName is truly NULL?
choices: LTRIM(NULL) returns NULL, so LEN(NULL) returns NULL too — which is not equal to 0, so that row would be missed by the whitespace check
The query would throw a syntax error immediately
SQL Server would automatically substitute an empty string on its own
It has no effect — NULL and '' behave identically in LEN()
questions.right: Right again — you're seeing this pattern everywhere now, which is exactly the point. NULL propagates through every function it touches until something explicitly converts it.
questions.wrong: You've seen this shape twice already in earlier lessons, so let's connect it: LTRIM(NULL) is NULL, and LEN(NULL) is NULL too — never 0. Without ISNULL converting it to '' first, a truly-NULL row would silently slip past a check that's specifically looking for a length of 0.

G01-T04.close: That's three lessons in a row where you've correctly reasoned through how NULL quietly breaks a naive check — that pattern is going to serve you well for the rest of this group. Ready to move to Partial Record, where we shift from single fields to scoring a whole row?

G01-T05.open: New shape of problem here — instead of one bad field, we're scoring an entire record for how complete it is overall. Let's see how the query pulls that off.

questions.q: Why does the solution use a CTE (CompletenessScore) instead of writing the 6-field CASE expression directly in both SELECT and WHERE?
choices: Writing it once and referencing FieldsPopulated afterward avoids repeating six CASE WHEN blocks and the risk of the two copies drifting apart
CTEs are required whenever more than 3 columns are used
A CTE makes the query run without needing a FROM clause
CTEs automatically cache results between separate query runs
questions.right: Exactly right — and that "drift" risk is a real one. If you'd written the six-field expression twice and later changed one copy but forgot the other, your displayed score and your filter would quietly disagree.
questions.wrong: Here's the practical reason: that scoring expression is long, and the naive version would need it written twice — once in SELECT, once in WHERE. A CTE computes it once, so both the number you show and the number you filter on are guaranteed to be the same value, not two copies that could silently drift apart.

questions.q: What does `SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER ()` compute in the summary query?
choices: The grand total of all rows across every group, calculated as a window function in the same pass as the per-group counts
A running total that resets for each new group
The average number of rows per group
It throws an error — COUNT(*) cannot be used inside SUM()
questions.right: Yes — that's a neat trick once you see it. One pass over the data gives you both each group's count AND the grand total needed for the percentage, no separate subquery required.
questions.wrong: This is a genuinely clever technique worth remembering: OVER() with no PARTITION BY tells SQL Server to compute that SUM across the entire result set, not per-group. So every row gets access to the grand total in the same query pass — no second subquery needed just to get a denominator for the percentage.

questions.q: A customer record has 4 out of 6 mandatory fields populated. Per the lesson's thresholds, what status is it given?
choices: Acceptable
Complete
Incomplete
Critical — nearly empty
questions.right: Correct — 4 lands right at the bottom edge of the Acceptable band. Good attention to the actual threshold numbers, not just the general idea.
questions.wrong: Worth locking in the actual numbers here: 6/6 is Complete, 4-5 is Acceptable, 2-3 is Incomplete, and 0-1 is Critical. A score of exactly 4 lands right at the start of the Acceptable range.

G01-T05.close: You've now built a full per-record completeness score from scratch, in your head — the CTE pattern, the window-function trick, and the threshold logic all in one lesson. That's a genuinely reusable pattern you'll see again in real work. Conditional Completeness is next, and it builds directly on today's ideas.

G01-T06.open: This one's a step up in subtlety — fields that are only sometimes required, depending on another field's value. Let's see if you can spot why that breaks a normal schema constraint.

questions.q: Why can't a database schema enforce a rule like "if PaymentMethod is 'Card', CardLastFour must be populated" the same way it enforces a plain NOT NULL constraint?
choices: Conditional rules depend on the value of another column, which is business logic rather than a fixed structural constraint the schema can express directly
SQL Server does not support conditional logic of any kind
NOT NULL constraints can only be applied to numeric columns
CardLastFour is always optional, so no rule is actually being broken
questions.right: Exactly — and that's precisely why these bugs slip through so easily in the wild. A plain NOT NULL is a fixed rule; "required only sometimes" depends on another column's live value, which most schemas simply can't express.
questions.wrong: Here's the distinction that makes this lesson matter: a NOT NULL constraint says "always required, no exceptions." This rule says "required only when another column has a specific value" — that's conditional logic, which typically lives in application code or a validation query, not the schema. That's exactly why it's invisible to a basic NULL check.

questions.q: What is the standard structure for detecting a conditional completeness violation in SQL?
choices: WHEN [trigger condition] AND [dependent field] IS NULL
WHEN [dependent field] IS NULL OR [trigger condition] IS NULL
WHERE [trigger condition] IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY [trigger condition] HAVING [dependent field] IS NULL
questions.right: Right — AND is the key word there. You need both halves true at once: the rule has to actually apply, AND the required field has to actually be missing.
questions.wrong: Worth getting this shape exactly right, since it's the template for every conditional check: you need AND, not OR. The trigger condition confirms the rule even applies to this row, and the dependent-field NULL check confirms it was actually violated. OR would flag rows where the rule never even applied in the first place.

questions.q: In the Orders example, what does a violation of "DiscountPct > 0 AND ApprovedBy IS NULL" actually represent in the business?
choices: A discount was applied to an order without a recorded approver — a potential fraud or process-control risk
An order that hasn't shipped yet
A customer who has never placed an order before
A product that is out of stock
questions.right: Yes — and that's worth sitting with for a second, because this is a fraud-control gap, not just a data quality nitpick. Someone gave away money without the required sign-off being on record.
questions.wrong: This is the real-world stakes of this rule: it means a discount got applied to an order with no approver on record. That's not just messy data — it's a process-control gap that could represent a discount nobody actually authorized.

G01-T06.close: You've just connected schema limitations to real business risk — that's exactly the kind of thinking that goes beyond "can I write the query" into "do I understand why it matters." Optional Field Population Rate is next, and it's a nice change of pace: less about finding errors, more about measuring what's usable.

G01-T07.open: Different flavor of question here — not every gap is an error. Sometimes it's just a density question: how usable is this optional field, really? Let's find out.

questions.q: How does "population rate" differ from a simple NULL rate?
choices: Population rate counts both NULLs and blank strings as missing, giving a more complete picture than a NULL-only count
Population rate only applies to numeric columns
They're the same metric with two different names
Population rate measures how many rows exist in the table, not column completeness
questions.right: Exactly — you're combining the lessons from earlier in this group. NULL rate alone tells only half the story; blank strings hide in the other half.
questions.wrong: This connects back to G01-T02 directly: a NULL-only check would miss blank strings entirely. A column with 10% NULLs and 5% blanks has 15% genuinely missing data — population rate is the metric that reflects the real, honest number.

questions.q: Why does the column-profile query stack six separate SELECTs with UNION ALL instead of one query that loops over all columns?
choices: Standard SQL cannot dynamically iterate over columns without resorting to dynamic SQL, so stacking explicit SELECTs is the transparent, auditable alternative
UNION ALL is the only way to use COUNT() in SQL Server
Looping over columns is against SQL syntax rules entirely
It's purely a stylistic choice with no functional reason
questions.right: Right — verbose but transparent beats clever but opaque here. Anyone can read six stacked SELECTs and verify each one; that's a real advantage when someone else has to trust your validation logic later.
questions.wrong: Here's the underlying constraint: plain SQL has no "for each column" loop. A dynamic SQL version could generate this automatically, but the explicit UNION ALL version — while it takes more lines — is something any teammate can read and verify column by column without trusting a generated string of SQL.

questions.q: The lesson sets population-rate ratings like 95%+ = Excellent and 60%+ = Acceptable. What does it say about where those specific cutoffs come from?
choices: They're example thresholds — the real cutoffs are business decisions that should be agreed with stakeholders, not universal rules
They are hard-coded ANSI SQL standards that apply to every table
They're generated automatically based on the table's row count
They only apply to the DOB column specifically
questions.right: Yes — and that's an important instinct to carry forward. The SQL never changes, but what counts as "good enough" absolutely should, depending on who's asking and why.
questions.wrong: Worth remembering as you apply this elsewhere: those percentages are illustrative, not universal law. A 60% population rate might be totally fine for a rough marketing segment but completely unacceptable for a regulated field — real thresholds belong to a conversation with the business, not a fixed rule in the query.

G01-T07.close: Nice shift in thinking there — you separated "this is broken" from "this is usable for what we need," which is a distinction a lot of people miss. Missing Expected Row is next, and it's the trickiest one yet in this group: rows that don't exist at all.

G01-T08.open: This is the one that trips people up the most, because everything you've learned so far assumes a row exists to inspect. What happens when the row itself is the thing that's missing?

questions.q: Why can't a standard NULL check ever detect that a cost centre failed to submit its October budget entry?
choices: There's no row at all to inspect — NULL checks examine values inside existing rows, but a missing submission means the row itself never got created
NULL checks only work on date columns, not budget amounts
The Transactions table doesn't support NULL checks by design
October is always excluded from validation queries by default
questions.right: Exactly right — and that's the conceptual leap this whole lesson is built around. Every check before this one looked inside a row. This one has to notice the row was never there to begin with.
questions.wrong: This is the big shift the whole lesson turns on: every check you've done so far in this group inspects a value inside an existing row. A missing budget submission means there's no row at all — nothing for a NULL check to even look at. You have to build a separate "expected" set and compare against it to notice the gap.

questions.q: What role does CROSS JOIN play in this pattern?
choices: It generates every combination of two dimensions (e.g. every month × every branch) to build the full "expected" set before comparing against what actually exists
It removes duplicate rows from the Transactions table
It's used to speed up the query by skipping unindexed columns
It converts the Branch column into a numeric ID
questions.right: Right — CROSS JOIN is doing the heavy lifting of imagination here, generating the complete "this is what should exist" grid before you ever compare it to reality.
questions.wrong: Think of CROSS JOIN as building the imaginary complete picture first: every month paired with every branch, whether or not it actually happened. That full grid is the "expected" set — the LEFT JOIN afterward is what reveals which of those expected combinations never actually showed up.

questions.q: In the LEFT JOIN pattern for finding missing rows, what does `WHERE a.MonthStart IS NULL` actually mean?
choices: The expected row had no match in the Actual set — meaning that month/branch combination never submitted data
The MonthStart column itself contains a literal NULL value in the Transactions table
The query found a formatting error in the date column
The join failed and returned an error
questions.right: Yes — you've got the anti-join pattern down. That NULL isn't data, it's the absence of a match, and that absence is exactly the signal you're hunting for.
questions.wrong: This is the classic anti-join trick, worth remembering by name: when a LEFT JOIN finds no matching row on the right side, every right-side column comes back NULL — not because the data is NULL, but because there was nothing to join to. Testing for that NULL is how you detect "this expected combination never actually happened."

G01-T08.close: That's the hardest concept in this whole group, and you worked through all three layers of it — why NULL checks are blind here, how CROSS JOIN builds the expected picture, and how the anti-join reveals the gap. Genuinely strong work. Truncated Value is next, and it's a lighter one after that.

G01-T09.open: Back to something more concrete now — values that got cut off mid-string with zero error raised. Let's see if you can spot the tell-tale signs.

questions.q: Why can a VARCHAR(100) column silently store a 250-character value as only 100 characters, with no error?
choices: In many SQL Server configurations, string values exceeding a column's length are silently truncated on insert rather than rejected
SQL Server automatically compresses long strings to fit any column
VARCHAR columns have no length limit at all
The 250-character value gets stored in a separate overflow table automatically
questions.right: Exactly — and that silence is the whole danger. No error, no warning, just quietly incomplete data sitting there for months until someone notices product names ending mid-word.
questions.wrong: Here's what's actually happening under the hood: without ANSI_WARNINGS raising an error (and it's not always on, especially in legacy systems or bulk loads), an over-length string just gets quietly cut down to fit. No error, no warning — the data is simply, permanently incomplete from that point on.

questions.q: Why is a value that lands exactly at a column's maximum length treated as a signal of possible truncation?
choices: It's not proof by itself, but a cluster of values all landing exactly at the boundary is a strong practical indicator that longer originals were cut off
SQL Server automatically flags any value at the max length as invalid
It means the column definition itself is wrong
Values at the exact max length always represent test data that should be deleted
questions.right: Right — and notice the careful wording: it's a signal, not proof. One value at the limit could be coincidence; a whole cluster at the exact same boundary is a real pattern.
questions.wrong: Worth being precise here — it's a signal, not a guarantee. One value naturally being exactly 50 characters could just be coincidence. But many rows all landing exactly at 50 is a strong pattern suggesting the true values were longer and got sliced off at that boundary.

questions.q: What advantage does querying `sys.columns` for the actual max_length give over hard-coding the number 50 in the query?
choices: The check stays accurate even if the column definition changes or differs between environments, instead of silently checking against a stale hard-coded number
sys.columns runs faster than any other system view
It automatically fixes truncated values without needing a rerun
It's required syntax — VARCHAR columns can't be queried without it
questions.right: Yes — and this is a maintainability lesson as much as a SQL one. A hard-coded 50 quietly goes stale the moment someone alters the column; reading the real definition never does.
questions.wrong: Think about what happens six months from now: a hard-coded 50 works only until someone alters the column, or the check runs against a different environment with a different size. Reading the real definition from sys.columns keeps the check accurate automatically, with no manual upkeep needed.

G01-T09.close: You've now got a genuinely practical eye for silent truncation — the boundary-clustering signal especially is something a lot of experienced people miss. Sentinel Default Value is next, and it rhymes with placeholder text from a few lessons back, but with its own twist.

G01-T10.open: This one connects straight back to Placeholder Text, but goes one layer deeper into why those specific values get chosen. Let's see the pattern.

questions.q: What is a "sentinel value" in the context of this lesson?
choices: A technically valid value (a real date or number) that a system uses to mean "unknown," chosen because it can't store an actual NULL
A value that SQL Server automatically rejects on insert
Any value greater than the column's maximum allowed size
A column-level security setting that restricts who can edit a field
questions.right: Exactly — the key word is technically valid. That's what makes sentinels so much harder to catch than a blank field: they pass right through every check that's just looking for something missing.
questions.wrong: Here's the core idea: a sentinel like 01/01/1900 or -1 is a real, storable value — it's just not a real answer. Older systems that couldn't store an actual NULL used a specific "magic" value to mean "we don't know this," and that old convention leaks into the data forever.

questions.q: Why might three systems feeding into the same table each have a different sentinel date for "unknown"?
choices: Different platforms have different minimum representable dates by design (e.g. SQL Server's minimum DATETIME vs Access's vs Excel's epoch), so each system's default "empty" date differs
Sentinel dates are randomly assigned by SQL Server at import time
Only one system is allowed to use sentinel values at a time
Sentinel dates change automatically based on the server's time zone
questions.right: Right — this is genuinely useful to know for real migrations. Each platform's own technical minimum becomes its unofficial "empty date" convention, and those conventions collide the moment systems start talking to each other.
questions.wrong: This is real-world data archaeology, worth remembering: each platform historically defaulted to its own technical minimum — SQL Server's earliest DATETIME, Access's earliest date, Excel's date-serial epoch. When systems built on different platforms feed the same table, their different "unknown" conventions collide with real data in different ways.

questions.q: What is the correct fix once a sentinel value has been identified, according to the lesson?
choices: Convert it to a real NULL at ingestion using NULLIF or a CASE WHEN, so downstream NULL-handling logic applies correctly
Delete every row that contains the sentinel value
Leave it as-is, since it's already a valid value the column accepts
Rename the column so the sentinel no longer applies
questions.right: Yes — turn it back into what it always secretly meant. Once it's a real NULL, every NULL-handling rule you already have downstream just works correctly, with no special-casing needed.
questions.wrong: The fix is to unmask it, not delete it: NULLIF(DOB, '19000101') — or an equivalent CASE WHEN — converts the sentinel back into a genuine NULL. That way, every downstream system's existing NULL-handling logic correctly treats it as missing, without needing to know about that specific legacy convention.

G01-T10.close: You've now got a real toolkit for the sneakiest completeness bug there is — values that look real, pass every basic check, and only reveal themselves once you know the source system's history. Incomplete Address is next, and it's a nice practical application of the scoring pattern from earlier.

G01-T11.open: This one brings together the scoring idea from Partial Record and applies it somewhere very concrete: can a parcel actually get delivered to this address?

questions.q: Why does the query use CONCAT to build a single "MissingComponents" string instead of returning one Y/N column per address field?
choices: It's easier for an operations team to action — they see exactly which components are missing in one readable string instead of scanning across several columns
CONCAT is required whenever more than 2 columns are compared
It makes the query run faster by reducing the number of columns returned
Y/N columns aren't supported for address data in SQL Server
questions.right: Exactly — you're thinking about the person who has to use this output, not just the person who wrote the query. That's a real skill, not just a technical one.
questions.wrong: Think about who reads this output at 8am with 800 parcels to sort: seeing "City PostCode" in one glance is much faster to act on than scanning across four separate Y/N flag columns and mentally piecing together which ones say 'missing'.

questions.q: Why is AddressLine2 deliberately excluded from the completeness score?
choices: It's optional by design (flat number, floor, suite) — flagging its absence would create false positives for every customer who legitimately doesn't need it
AddressLine2 doesn't exist as a real column in most systems
Including it would make the query too slow to run
SQL Server doesn't allow optional fields to be checked for completeness
questions.right: Right — and this is an important discipline: not every empty field is a problem. Scoring an optional field as "missing" for everyone who legitimately doesn't need it would just create noise.
questions.wrong: This is about knowing which fields are actually optional: most addresses genuinely don't need a second line. Scoring it as "missing" for every customer without one would flood the results with false positives on a field that was never required in the first place.

questions.q: The lesson says address completeness rules are "domain-specific." What does that mean in practice?
choices: What counts as a "complete enough" address depends on the use case — a courier needs PostCode + Country, while marketing might only need City
Every company must use the exact same 4-field address standard by law
Address completeness only matters for international customers
The rules change automatically based on which country the customer is in
questions.right: Yes — same instinct you showed back in the population-rate lesson. The mechanics of the query stay the same; what counts as "good enough" is a decision made by whoever's going to actually use the data.
questions.wrong: This echoes what you saw in Optional Field Population Rate: the required-field set and the score threshold should be configured per use case, not treated as one universal rule. A courier's routing needs (PostCode + Country) are stricter than a marketing segmentation use case, which might only need City.

G01-T11.close: You've now applied the completeness-scoring pattern to a genuinely practical business problem — dispatch failures cost real money, and this is exactly the kind of check that prevents them. One lesson left in this group: Missing Child Records.

G01-T12.open: Last one in the Completeness group — and it's a nice bridge into the next topic, since it's about relationships between tables, not just single columns.

questions.q: What's the key difference between using NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... WHERE ... IS NULL to find customers with no orders?
choices: They find the same rows; NOT EXISTS can be faster on large indexed tables since it stops at the first match, while LEFT JOIN materializes the full join first
NOT EXISTS only works on numeric columns
LEFT JOIN can never be used to find missing child records
NOT EXISTS requires a completely different table structure
questions.right: Exactly — same result, different performance character. NOT EXISTS can bail out early the moment it finds one match; LEFT JOIN builds the whole join first and filters after.
questions.wrong: Good news: both patterns return identical results here, so this is about performance and clarity, not correctness. NOT EXISTS often performs better on large, well-indexed child tables because it can stop scanning as soon as one match is found — the LEFT JOIN version builds out the full join before it ever filters.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call "a customer with no orders" a business completeness check rather than a schema violation?
choices: A brand-new customer legitimately exists before placing their first order, so the schema can't and shouldn't forbid that state — it's a business question of how long is too long, not a structural rule
Schema constraints can only apply to numeric columns
Customers and Orders are always in different databases
SQL Server doesn't support foreign key constraints between these tables
questions.right: Right — and this echoes something you already worked out back in Conditional Completeness: some rules are structural, and some are genuinely about business timing, not database design.
questions.wrong: This connects to the schema-vs-business-logic idea from a few lessons back: a schema constraint would make "customer without an order" impossible to create at all — but that's a completely normal state right after sign-up. The real business question isn't "can this exist" but "how many days without an order should trigger outreach."

questions.q: What does grouping customers into order bands (0, 1, 2-5, 6+) add beyond just listing the zero-order customers?
choices: It gives business context — showing what percentage of the whole customer base is inactive, not just a raw list with no sense of scale
It automatically fixes the missing-order problem
It's required before NOT EXISTS can be used
It converts the CustomerID column into a different data type
questions.right: Yes — a raw list has no sense of scale on its own. Seeing it next to the other bands tells you immediately whether this is a minor edge case or a real chunk of your customer base.
questions.wrong: Think about what a bare list of zero-order customers is missing: it doesn't tell you if that's 2% or 40% of the whole base. Seeing it next to the 1-order and 2-5-order bands gives that missing sense of scale — how significant is the inactive segment, really?

G01-T12.close: That's the full Completeness group done — twelve lessons, and you've built real instincts for NULLs, blanks, placeholders, sentinels, missing rows, and missing relationships. That's a genuinely strong foundation for everything else in Data Validation. Nicely done.

G02-T01.open: Welcome to Group 2 — Uniqueness. Completeness asked "is the data there?" This group asks a different question: "does it appear more than once when it shouldn't?" Let's start with the simplest case: rows that are exact copies of each other.

questions.q: Why does the GROUP BY in this query deliberately exclude CustomerID, the surrogate key, when looking for exact duplicate rows?
choices: Because CustomerID is unique by definition, so grouping on it would never find a group with more than one row — the goal is content duplicates, not key duplicates
Because CustomerID is a reserved column name in SQL Server
Because surrogate keys cannot be used in GROUP BY clauses
Because it would make the query run slower
questions.right: Exactly — and this is the whole trick of the lesson in one line. Group on the surrogate key and every group has exactly one row, always, because that's what a surrogate key guarantees. You have to group on the business columns instead to find rows that are really the same.
questions.wrong: Here's the reasoning: CustomerID is auto-generated and unique by design — every row already has its own value, so grouping on it would put every single row in its own group of one, and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 would never fire. The whole point is to find rows that are duplicates in content, so the GROUP BY has to run on the business columns (name, email, phone, etc.), not the key that's guaranteed unique.

questions.q: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY CustomerID ASC)` is used to rank rows within each duplicate group. What does RowRank = 1 represent?
choices: The row with the lowest CustomerID in that duplicate group — treated as the original to keep
The row that was most recently updated
A random row selected for deletion
The row with the most populated fields
questions.right: Right — ORDER BY CustomerID ASC inside the PARTITION means the earliest-created row always lands at rank 1, and everything ranked 2 or higher in that same group is a candidate for deletion.
questions.wrong: The ORDER BY inside PARTITION BY controls the ranking: ASC on CustomerID means the row with the smallest (earliest) ID gets RowRank 1 in each duplicate group, treated as the master record to keep. Every other row in that same group — RowRank 2, 3, and so on — is a duplicate candidate.

questions.q: The lesson's explanation insists on "always SELECT before DELETE." What is that step actually protecting against?
choices: Running the DELETE against the wrong set of rows without ever having verified which IDs would actually be removed
SQL Server syntax errors in the DELETE statement
Slow query performance on large tables
Losing the CustomerID column's data type
questions.right: Yes — and this a habit worth keeping for life, not just this lesson. A DELETE is one keystroke away from a SELECT that filters the same rows. Running the SELECT first and actually reading the row count and the IDs is the only real safeguard before something irreversible runs.
questions.wrong: The point isn't syntax or performance — it's irreversibility. A DELETE with the wrong WHERE clause removes real data with no undo. Running the equivalent SELECT first, and actually looking at which rows and how many would be affected, is the only way to catch a mistake before it's permanent instead of after.

G02-T01.close: Good start on Uniqueness — you've got the core distinction locked in: group on content, not on the key that's guaranteed unique, and always look before you delete. Duplicate Primary Key is next, and it's a sharper version of the same idea.

G02-T02.open: This lesson asks what happens when the thing that's SUPPOSED to guarantee uniqueness — the primary key itself — has been bypassed.

questions.q: What does `COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT ProductID)` actually tell you?
choices: The exact number of extra (duplicate) rows sitting on top of what a truly unique key would produce
The total number of products in the table
The number of NULL values in ProductID
The average number of duplicates per product
questions.right: Exactly — COUNT(*) counts every row, COUNT(DISTINCT ProductID) counts each value once, and the gap between them is precisely how many duplicate rows exist. Zero gap means the column behaves as a real key, constraint or no constraint.
questions.wrong: Break it into its two halves: COUNT(*) is every row in the table. COUNT(DISTINCT ProductID) is how many unique key values exist. Subtract one from the other and what's left is exactly the number of extra rows beyond what a truly unique key would have — the duplicate count, with no need for a separate GROUP BY.

questions.q: Inside the duplicate-ranking CTE, why does the lesson use `ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)` instead of ordering by a real column?
choices: It signals there is no reliable basis for choosing which duplicate row to keep — that decision needs a human or a business rule, not a sort
It is required syntax whenever ROW_NUMBER() is used
It makes the query run without a PARTITION BY clause
It automatically picks the row with the highest price
questions.right: Right — it's a deliberate statement, not a placeholder. `ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)` means "I'm not claiming any of these rows is more correct than another," which is honest when the duplicate rows genuinely have no natural tiebreaker.
questions.wrong: This one is about honesty in the query, not mechanics: `ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)` means there's no column that meaningfully decides which duplicate is the "real" one — different prices on the same ProductID don't tell you which price is correct. Rather than picking arbitrarily and hiding that choice, the query flags that a human decision is needed.

questions.q: What real operational mistake caused the 7 duplicate ProductCode rows in the lesson's scenario?
choices: Constraints were disabled for a bulk load (NOCHECK CONSTRAINT) and never re-enabled afterward
The ProductCode column was accidentally deleted and recreated
Two different databases were merged without any migration script
SQL Server has a known bug that duplicates primary keys under heavy load
questions.right: Yes — a very common real-world cause. Disabling constraints to speed up a bulk load is a normal DBA move; forgetting the re-enable step afterward is what turns it into a live bug.
questions.wrong: Per the lesson: a DBA ran `ALTER TABLE ... NOCHECK CONSTRAINT ALL` to speed up a bulk load — a legitimate technique — but never re-enabled the constraint afterward. With the PK constraint off, nothing stopped duplicate ProductCodes from being inserted, and they were, silently.

G02-T02.close: You've now seen that a primary key is only as strong as whether its constraint is actually enforced right now — not whether one was ever defined. Duplicate Natural / Business Key is next: what happens when the surrogate key is fine but the real-world identifier isn't.

G02-T03.open: This lesson makes a distinction that trips up a lot of people the first time they see it: your primary key can be perfectly unique while your data is still full of duplicates. Let's see why.

questions.q: What is the difference between a surrogate key and a natural key, and why doesn't surrogate-key uniqueness guarantee natural-key uniqueness?
choices: A surrogate key (like an auto-increment ID) is system-generated and always unique by construction; a natural key (like Email) is a real-world identifier the system never enforces uniqueness on unless you explicitly check it
They are two names for the same concept
A natural key is always numeric and a surrogate key is always text
Surrogate keys are only used in NoSQL databases
questions.right: Exactly right — and this is the core idea of the whole lesson. CustomerID being unique tells you nothing about whether Email is unique, because the database never promised that for Email in the first place.
questions.wrong: Here's the distinction: CustomerID is a surrogate key — the system generates it and guarantees it's unique, that's its whole job. Email is a natural key — a real-world identifier that's supposed to be unique in the business sense, but nothing in the schema enforces that unless a separate constraint or check exists. One being unique says nothing about the other.

questions.q: What does adding `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY Email)` inside the CTE give you, that a separate subquery would have taken an extra step to produce?
choices: TotalSharing — the count of how many customers share that email, available on every row in the same pass, without a second query
The total number of rows in the entire Customers table
A random sample of duplicate rows
The average CustomerID per email
questions.right: Right — a window function computes that count alongside every row in the same query, so you can filter on it (WHERE TotalSharing > 1) and display it, without a separate COUNT subquery joined back in.
questions.wrong: Without the window function, you'd need a separate subquery to count how many rows share each email, then join that count back to the main query. `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY Email)` computes and attaches that count to every row directly, in the same single pass — that's the efficiency window functions buy you here.

questions.q: The lesson ranks the earliest CustomerID as the "original" record to keep. According to the explanation, is that ranking a hard rule?
choices: No — it's a starting point; the real decision depends on which record has more complete data, was more recently active, or which system is authoritative, and a human or business rule makes the final call
Yes — the earliest record is always legally the correct one to keep
No — the newest record should always be kept instead
The ranking is chosen at random each time the query runs
questions.right: Exactly — the query surfaces the candidates and a sensible default ordering, but it doesn't claim to know which record is actually "right." That's explicitly left as a human or business-rule decision.
questions.wrong: The lesson is direct about this: "the convention of keeping the lowest CustomerID is a starting point — not a rule." The validation query's job is to surface which records are candidates; deciding which one is actually correct depends on data completeness, recency, or which system is the source of truth — a call for a human, not the query.

G02-T03.close: The surrogate-vs-natural-key distinction you just built is one you'll use constantly — a clean primary key tells you nothing about whether the data underneath it is trustworthy. Near-Duplicate (Fuzzy Match) is next, where even the natural key itself isn't spelled the same way twice.

G02-T04.open: So far every duplicate has been an exact match on some column. This lesson is different — what if the same person was entered twice, just spelled slightly differently each time?

questions.q: In the self-join pattern `FROM Customers A JOIN Customers B ON ... AND A.CustomerID < B.CustomerID`, why is the `<` condition there?
choices: Without it, every matching pair would appear twice — once as (A,B) and once as (B,A) — the less-than condition keeps each pair to a single row
It filters out customers who joined more recently
It's required to make SOUNDEX() work correctly
It excludes customers with a CustomerID below 100
questions.right: Exactly — a self-join naturally produces both (1,11) and (11,1) for the same pair, since the join has no sense of direction. `A.CustomerID < B.CustomerID` breaks that symmetry so each real pair shows up exactly once.
questions.wrong: Think about what a self-join without that condition produces: every matching pair would show up twice, as (1,11) and again as (11,1) — same people, same match, listed twice. Requiring A's ID to be strictly less than B's ID keeps only one direction of each pair, so duplicates in the *output* don't multiply on top of the duplicates you're trying to find.

questions.q: What does the `DIFFERENCE()` function's score of 0 to 4 actually measure?
choices: How similar two strings' SOUNDEX codes are — 4 means the codes are identical (sounds the same), 0 means no similarity
The number of characters that differ between two strings
How many rows match a given WHERE condition
The alphabetical distance between two strings
questions.right: Right — DIFFERENCE() compares SOUNDEX codes, not raw strings. A score of 4 is the strongest phonetic similarity signal, and 3 or 4 is generally treated as a strong duplicate candidate.
questions.wrong: DIFFERENCE() doesn't compare the letters directly — it compares the SOUNDEX codes of two strings and scores how similar those codes are, from 0 (no similarity) to 4 (essentially identical sounding). It's a similarity score layered on top of SOUNDEX, not a separate string-distance measure.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the correct next step after SOUNDEX/DIFFERENCE surface a list of near-duplicate candidates?
choices: Narrow by a second corroborating attribute, then have a human review or automated scoring confirm the match before any MERGE happens
Immediately delete every candidate pair automatically
Ignore the candidates since phonetic matching is never reliable
Merge all candidates without review since SOUNDEX is exact
questions.right: Yes — candidates are a starting point, not a verdict. The lesson is explicit that phonetic matches need a second attribute and human or automated confirmation before anything gets merged.
questions.wrong: The lesson spells out the process directly: (1) generate candidates via phonetic matching, (2) narrow using a second corroborating attribute like matching DOB or postcode, (3) get human review or automated scoring to actually confirm the match, (4) only then MERGE. SOUNDEX and DIFFERENCE are heuristics — they suggest, they don't decide.

G02-T04.close: You've now got the full fuzzy-matching workflow, not just the SQL — generate candidates, narrow with a second signal, confirm before acting. Phonetic Duplicate (SOUNDEX Match) is next, going one level deeper into how SOUNDEX actually encodes a name.

G02-T05.open: Let's go one level deeper into SOUNDEX itself — not just using it, but understanding what it actually does and where it breaks down.

questions.q: SOUNDEX matching on last name alone tends to produce a lot of false positives (e.g. every "Smith" variant matching every other "Smith" variant). What does this lesson add to cut that down?
choices: Requiring the same first-name initial and the same country alongside the SOUNDEX match, narrowing the candidate list while still catching the real cases
Switching from SOUNDEX to an exact string match instead
Removing the JOIN entirely and using a WHERE clause only
Only checking customers created in the last 30 days
questions.right: Exactly — SOUNDEX alone casts a wide net on purpose. Adding a second and third condition (first initial, country) is what turns a noisy candidate list into something actually usable.
questions.wrong: SOUNDEX by itself is deliberately loose — it's built to catch phonetic variants, which means it also catches a lot of unrelated people who just happen to have similar-sounding last names. Requiring the first-name initial to match too, and the country to match, dramatically narrows the false positives while keeping the real matches.

questions.q: Per the lesson's explanation of the SOUNDEX algorithm, what does it deliberately ignore when encoding a name?
choices: Vowels, and the letters H and W
The first letter of the name
Numbers embedded in the name
Capitalization
questions.right: Right — SOUNDEX keeps the first letter as-is, then encodes the consonants that follow into digit groups, skipping vowels and H/W entirely. That's exactly why phonetically similar spellings can still collapse to the same code.
questions.wrong: Per the algorithm described in the lesson: SOUNDEX keeps the first letter of the name, then walks through the rest encoding consonants into digit groups (B/F/P/V=1, C/G/J/K/Q/S/X/Z=2, D/T=3, L=4, M/N=5, R=6) — vowels and the letters H and W are skipped entirely during that encoding.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call SOUNDEX a poor fit for multilingual datasets?
choices: SOUNDEX was designed specifically for English names and performs poorly on Arabic, Chinese, Hindi, or other non-English names
SOUNDEX only works with names shorter than 4 characters
SOUNDEX cannot be used on any column that allows NULL values
SOUNDEX requires a separate license for non-English datasets
questions.right: Yes — it's baked into how the algorithm was designed, not a technical limitation you can configure around. The lesson points at METAPHONE or Levenshtein-distance approaches (e.g. via Python's jellyfish) as better fits for multilingual data.
questions.wrong: SOUNDEX's encoding rules were built around English phonetics and spelling conventions specifically — so it simply doesn't model how names sound or vary in other languages well. For multilingual datasets the lesson points at alternatives like METAPHONE or Levenshtein-distance libraries (e.g. Python's jellyfish) instead.

G02-T05.close: You've now got a real, working knowledge of SOUNDEX — not just calling the function, but knowing what it encodes, what it ignores, and where it stops being useful. Composite Key Duplicate is next: uniqueness that only reveals itself when you combine two or three columns together.

G02-T06.open: New shape of problem: sometimes no single column is unique, and no single column being checked alone will ever catch the bug. Let's see why.

questions.q: In the payroll scenario, checking CustomerID alone or TransactionDate alone would find nothing wrong. Why does the composite (CustomerID, TransactionDate, Amount) reveal the duplicate that neither column alone can?
choices: Each individual column is expected to repeat many times normally — the problem only exists in the specific combination of all three appearing together more than once
SQL Server cannot check single columns for duplicates at all
TransactionDate is stored as text, so it can't be grouped on its own
CustomerID and Amount are the same data type, causing a conflict
questions.right: Exactly — the same customer appearing many times is completely normal, and the same date appearing many times is completely normal. The bug only exists in the specific combination happening twice, which is invisible to any single-column check.
questions.wrong: This is the central idea of composite keys: CustomerID repeating is fine (customers make many transactions), and TransactionDate repeating is fine (lots of transactions happen on the same day). The actual problem — this customer having the same amount twice on the same date — only becomes visible when you group on all three columns together, not any one of them alone.

questions.q: What does `PARTITION BY CustomerID, TransactionDate, Amount` inside ROW_NUMBER() actually do?
choices: Restarts the row numbering for every unique combination of those three values, so any combination appearing more than once gets rows numbered 2, 3, etc.
Sorts the entire table by CustomerID only
Deletes rows where any of the three columns is NULL
Merges the three columns into a single new column
questions.right: Right — PARTITION BY with multiple columns groups on the combination of all of them, and ROW_NUMBER restarts at 1 within each group. Anything at rank 2 or higher shares an identical combination with an earlier row.
questions.wrong: PARTITION BY with several columns listed treats the *combination* of those values as the grouping key — every row sharing the same CustomerID, TransactionDate, and Amount together gets numbered starting from 1 within that specific group. A second occurrence of the same combination gets rank 2, which is exactly the duplicate.

questions.q: The lesson notes that maybe two $250 charges on the same day are legitimate (morning and evening). What does this tell you about defining a composite key?
choices: What columns together form "the key" is a business decision, not a fixed SQL rule — the query pattern stays the same, only the GROUP BY columns change based on that decision
Composite keys should never include a monetary amount column
SQL Server automatically detects the correct composite key for any table
Two transactions on the same day are always an error regardless of amount
questions.right: Exactly — the SQL technique is reusable, but which columns actually define "shouldn't repeat" is a call only the business can make, not something the query can determine on its own.
questions.wrong: The lesson is explicit: "what constitutes a composite key is a business decision." The SQL pattern — GROUP BY the chosen columns, HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 — never changes. What changes is which columns you decide belong in that GROUP BY, and that decision has to come from understanding the business process, not from the query itself.

G02-T06.close: You've now separated the SQL technique (which never changes) from the business decision of which columns define uniqueness (which always does). Conditional Duplicate is next — uniqueness that only applies to a subset of rows, not the whole table.

G02-T07.open: Here's a rule that sounds contradictory at first: a customer can have two contracts, just not two of the same kind at the same time. Let's see how a WHERE clause turns "sometimes unique" into something checkable.

questions.q: What single addition turns a normal duplicate check into a conditional uniqueness check?
choices: A WHERE clause (e.g. WHERE IsActive = 1) placed before the GROUP BY, restricting the duplicate check to only the subset of rows the uniqueness rule actually applies to
Replacing GROUP BY with ORDER BY
Adding a UNIQUE constraint with no WHERE clause
Using SELECT DISTINCT instead of GROUP BY
questions.right: Exactly — the WHERE clause is what makes it conditional. Filter to only active rows first, then GROUP BY within that subset, and historical or cancelled rows never enter the check at all.
questions.wrong: The key move is filtering *before* grouping: adding `WHERE IsActive = 1` (or `WHERE Status = 'Active'`) restricts the entire duplicate check to only the rows where the uniqueness rule actually applies. Historical records outside that condition are excluded from the check entirely, which is exactly what makes the rule conditional rather than universal.

questions.q: Why can't a plain UNIQUE constraint enforce "only one active role per department," and what SQL feature can?
choices: A standard UNIQUE constraint applies across all rows unconditionally; a filtered unique index (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE IsActive = 1) enforces uniqueness only within the active subset
UNIQUE constraints only work on numeric columns
SQL Server has no way to enforce conditional uniqueness at the database level
A CHECK constraint should be used instead of any index
questions.right: Right — a plain UNIQUE constraint has no concept of "only when a condition is true," it just blocks any duplicate value everywhere. A filtered unique index with its own WHERE clause is what actually enforces conditional uniqueness at the database level.
questions.wrong: A standard UNIQUE constraint has no awareness of conditions — it blocks duplicates everywhere in the table, full stop, which would make historical/inactive rows impossible to keep. The database-level fix is a filtered unique index — `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON Employees (Department, EmployeeID) WHERE IsActive = 1` — which only enforces uniqueness among the rows matching that WHERE clause.

questions.q: In the CTE, the PARTITION BY only sees rows where IsActive = 1 was already applied. What does this mean for historical (non-active) rows?
choices: They are excluded from the CTE entirely, so the ranking and duplicate check never considers them at all — only active rows compete for rank within their partition
They are included but always ranked last
They cause the query to throw an error
They are automatically converted to active rows
questions.right: Exactly — filtering happens before the window function runs, so the ranking logic literally never sees the historical rows. They're not ranked low, they're not in the data at all by the time PARTITION BY runs.
questions.wrong: Because the WHERE IsActive = 1 filter is applied inside the CTE before the ROW_NUMBER() window function runs, the historical rows are gone by the time PARTITION BY does its work — they're not part of the partition, not ranked, not considered at all. Only rows that passed the active filter compete for rank within their group.

G02-T07.close: Conditional uniqueness — filter first, then group — is a pattern you'll reuse constantly once you notice how many real-world rules are secretly "unique, but only among the active/current rows." Cross-Table Duplicate is next: what happens when the same entity lives in two completely different tables.

G02-T08.open: Every duplicate so far has lived inside one table. This lesson asks: what if the same real person exists in two different tables entirely, under two different keys?

questions.q: Why does the query wrap both sides of the email comparison in `UPPER(LTRIM(RTRIM(...)))` before joining the two tables?
choices: To prevent purely cosmetic differences — case, leading/trailing spaces — from causing genuine matches to be missed, since two systems rarely store the same email identically
Because JOIN clauses require all text columns to be uppercase
To make the query run faster on large tables
Because email addresses cannot contain lowercase letters
questions.right: Exactly — two independently-built systems will format the same email slightly differently more often than not. Normalizing both sides the same way before comparing is what catches the real matches that case or whitespace would otherwise hide.
questions.wrong: This is about matching across two systems that were never designed to agree on formatting: one system might store 'John@Email.com', the other 'john@email.com '. Neither difference means the emails are actually different — normalizing both sides with UPPER(LTRIM(RTRIM(...))) before comparing prevents those cosmetic differences from causing a real match to be missed.

questions.q: In this cross-table pattern, what does an INNER JOIN between the two tables on the matching key actually return?
choices: Only the rows that exist in both tables — exactly the intersection needed to find entities present in both
Every row from both tables, with NULLs where there's no match
Only rows that exist in the first table but not the second
A random sample of rows from each table
questions.right: Right — INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides, which is precisely the definition of "exists in both tables" that cross-table duplicate detection needs.
questions.wrong: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the join condition matches on both sides — the intersection of the two tables. That's exactly what "who appears in both tables" needs: LEFT JOIN would instead give you everything from one side plus NULLs where there's no match, which answers a different question.

questions.q: The lesson explicitly says finding someone in both Customers and Employees "is not always an error." What does it identify as a legitimate reason for the overlap?
choices: An employee who is also a customer of the company — a normal, expected business scenario
A database backup that accidentally duplicated all rows
A bug in the JOIN syntax that always produces false matches
Two employees who happen to share the same manager
questions.right: Yes — the lesson is careful to distinguish this from a bug. An employee who's also a customer is completely normal; the query's real value is checking whether their details agree across the two systems, not flagging the overlap itself as wrong.
questions.wrong: Per the lesson: "an employee who is also a customer is a legitimate business case — it's expected." The cross-table match by itself isn't the problem; what the query goes on to check is whether the details are *consistent* between the two records — a name or DOB mismatch is the actual thing worth investigating, not the overlap.

G02-T08.close: You've now handled duplicates within a table, within a filtered subset, and across two entirely separate tables. Duplicate with Different Surrogate Key is next — the case where even the ID itself is no protection at all.

G02-T09.open: Here's an uncomfortable fact this lesson wants you to sit with: a perfectly enforced, unique primary key can still let a table fill up with duplicates. Let's see how.

questions.q: The lesson states plainly: a unique PK does NOT mean no duplicates. What does a PK constraint actually guarantee, and what does it say nothing about?
choices: It guarantees every row has a unique identifier; it says nothing about whether the row's actual content (name, price, category) duplicates another row's content
It guarantees the table has no more than 1000 rows
It guarantees every column in the row is non-NULL
It guarantees the table cannot be joined to another table
questions.right: Exactly — a PK constraint's entire job is preventing two rows from sharing the same ID value. It has no opinion at all about whether the content in those rows is otherwise identical.
questions.wrong: A PK constraint on ProductID only prevents two rows from both being ProductID = P001 — that's its complete job. It cannot and does not prevent two rows with different auto-generated IDs from having identical ProductName, Category, and Price. Unique identity and unique content are two completely separate guarantees.

questions.q: What does `CHECKSUM(col1, col2, col3)` do, and what limitation does the lesson flag about it?
choices: It generates an integer hash fingerprinting the combined column values so identical content produces identical checksums — but it has a small collision risk where different content can occasionally produce the same hash
It counts how many columns are NULL in a row
It permanently deletes rows with matching checksums
It only works on integer columns, never text
questions.right: Right — CHECKSUM is a fast fingerprint for finding likely content duplicates, but it's not collision-proof. For anything where a false match would be costly, the lesson points at HASHBYTES('SHA2_256', ...) instead.
questions.wrong: CHECKSUM combines several column values into a single integer hash — rows with identical content produce identical checksums, which is a fast way to spot candidate duplicates. The catch the lesson flags: it has a small collision risk, where two genuinely *different* rows could occasionally produce the same checksum by chance. For higher-stakes deduplication, HASHBYTES('SHA2_256', ...) is the collision-resistant alternative.

questions.q: What is the root-cause fix the lesson recommends for a pipeline that keeps creating reload duplicates?
choices: Replace the INSERT-only pipeline with MERGE, which updates existing matching rows instead of always inserting new ones
Add more auto-increment columns to the table
Run the pipeline less frequently
Disable the primary key constraint entirely
questions.right: Yes — the actual bug lives in the pipeline logic, not the table. INSERT-only means every run creates new rows regardless of whether the data already exists; MERGE checks first and updates instead of blindly inserting.
questions.wrong: The lesson identifies the root cause directly: an INSERT-only pipeline creates a new row every time it runs, whether or not that data already exists. MERGE is the fix — it checks whether a matching row already exists (by a real key like ProductCode) and updates it if so, only inserting when the row is genuinely new.

G02-T09.close: You've now seen the sharpest version of "unique key, duplicate data" this group has to offer. Soft-Delete Duplicate is next — the last lesson in this group, and it combines conditional uniqueness with a pattern you'll see in almost every real production system.

G02-T10.open: Last lesson in Uniqueness. Soft deletes are everywhere in real systems — let's see how they can quietly let a duplicate slip through even when everyone did almost everything right.

questions.q: Why can't a standard UNIQUE constraint on Email work in a table that uses soft deletes?
choices: A re-subscribed customer's old, soft-deleted row still holds their email, so a standard UNIQUE constraint would block the new row from ever being inserted
Soft-deleted tables cannot have any constraints at all
Email columns are never allowed to have UNIQUE constraints in SQL Server
It would work fine — there is no actual problem
questions.right: Exactly — the old row never physically leaves the table, it just gets flagged. A plain UNIQUE constraint doesn't care about that flag, so it would block a legitimate re-subscription from ever being created.
questions.wrong: Here's the conflict: in a soft-delete system, a cancelled customer's row is never removed — it's just flagged IsActive = 0 and kept forever as history. If Email had a plain UNIQUE constraint, that old flagged row would still occupy the email value, and the customer's genuine re-subscription (a new row with the same email) would be rejected as a duplicate, even though it's exactly what should happen.

questions.q: In Step 4's classification, what does "Expected: Active + history" mean for a given email?
choices: Exactly one active record plus one or more soft-deleted records — the normal, correct pattern after a cancel-then-resubscribe cycle, not a bug
The customer's data is corrupted and needs manual repair
The email appears in both the Customers and Employees tables
The record has never been modified since creation
questions.right: Right — this is the state the system is supposed to produce after a normal cancel-and-return. It's specifically distinguished from the actual bug (multiple active records), which is the real problem.
questions.wrong: This classification means: exactly one row where IsActive = 1 (the current subscription) plus one or more rows where IsActive = 0 (cancelled history) — which is precisely what a correctly-working cancel-then-resubscribe flow should produce. The lesson's whole point is distinguishing this normal state from the actual bug: two rows both flagged active at once.

questions.q: What real operational impact does the bug (two active records for the same customer) actually cause?
choices: Every operation that filters WHERE IsActive = 1 runs twice for that customer — two emails sent, two payments taken, two role assignments granted
The customer's account is permanently locked
The database refuses to accept any new inserts
It has no real impact since the data is only used for reporting
questions.right: Yes — this is why the severity is rated Critical. Every downstream process that trusts "IsActive = 1 means exactly one row" silently runs twice for this customer, and nothing throws an error to reveal it.
questions.wrong: Because so much application logic filters on WHERE IsActive = 1 and assumes that returns one row per entity, having two active rows means every one of those operations quietly executes twice for the same customer — two billing emails, two payment attempts, two role grants — with no error anywhere to flag that something's wrong.

G02-T10.close: That's the full Uniqueness group — ten lessons, and you've gone from exact-copy rows all the way to soft-delete edge cases, with the fuzzy-matching and conditional-uniqueness patterns in between. Those cover the two biggest ideas in this whole group: sometimes uniqueness only applies to a subset of rows, and sometimes what looks like the same thing twice isn't spelled the same way at all. Strong session.

G03-T01.open: Group 3: Referential Integrity. Completeness asked "is it there," Uniqueness asked "does it repeat," — this group asks "do the connections between tables actually hold up." We'll start with the classic case: a row pointing at a parent that isn't there.

questions.q: In the LEFT JOIN pattern for finding orphan orders, what does filtering `WHERE c.CustomerID IS NULL` actually isolate?
choices: Rows from Orders that found no matching row in Customers — the LEFT JOIN fills the unmatched side with NULL, so filtering on that NULL isolates exactly the orphans
Rows where the CustomerID column itself contains a literal NULL value
Every row in the Orders table regardless of whether it matches
Rows where the CustomerID appears more than once
questions.right: Exactly — LEFT JOIN keeps every row from Orders and fills in Customers columns where a match exists, NULL where it doesn't. Filtering on that NULL is how you isolate exactly the rows with no matching parent.
questions.wrong: This is the anti-join pattern from Data Validation's earlier groups, applied to a real FK: LEFT JOIN keeps every Orders row and attaches Customers columns when a match exists. Where there's no match, those Customers columns come back NULL — not because CustomerID is NULL, but because nothing matched. Filtering `WHERE c.CustomerID IS NULL` isolates exactly those unmatched rows.

questions.q: The lesson presents both a LEFT JOIN version and a NOT EXISTS version for finding the same orphans. What's the actual tradeoff between them?
choices: They return identical rows; NOT EXISTS can be faster on large indexed tables since it stops at the first match, while LEFT JOIN is more convenient when checking multiple parent tables in one query
NOT EXISTS only works on numeric columns
LEFT JOIN cannot be used with more than one table
NOT EXISTS returns different rows than LEFT JOIN
questions.right: Right — same result set, different shape and performance character. This exact tradeoff came up back in Data Validation's Uniqueness group too, for the same underlying reason: both patterns answer "does a match exist," just phrased differently.
questions.wrong: Both patterns return the same rows. The practical difference: NOT EXISTS can short-circuit as soon as it finds one match, which tends to perform well on large, indexed parent tables. LEFT JOIN is convenient when you need to check against more than one parent table at once — Method A here checks Customers AND Products in a single query using two LEFT JOINs.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend Method C — a single count per FK relationship — for a data quality dashboard specifically?
choices: A single number per FK check that reads zero when healthy and turns non-zero when something breaks is exactly the kind of metric a dashboard can monitor and alert on
Method C is the only version that actually works correctly
Dashboards cannot display row-level detail, only counts
It hides which specific rows are affected, which is required for GDPR
questions.right: Exactly — Methods A and B are for investigating a known problem; Method C is for noticing one exists in the first place. A dashboard needs a number that's boring when things are fine and impossible to miss when they're not.
questions.wrong: Methods A and B give you the detail — which rows, which values. Method C compresses that down to one number per relationship, which is exactly what a monitoring dashboard needs: zero means clean, any non-zero triggers investigation. You'd use Method C to notice a problem exists, then Method A or B to actually dig into it.

G03-T01.close: The LEFT JOIN / NOT EXISTS anti-join pattern is the single most reusable technique in this entire group — you'll see it again in almost every lesson that follows. Dangling Reference is next: what happens when the parent existed, and was deleted later.

G03-T02.open: Same broken-connection symptom as the last lesson, different cause. This lesson asks you to separate "never had a valid parent" from "had one, and it got deleted."

questions.q: The lesson draws a distinction between an orphan (G03-T01) and a dangling reference (this lesson). What's the actual difference, given that both look identical in SQL?
choices: An orphan had an invalid FK from the start (bad data on creation); a dangling reference was valid when created but became invalid later because the parent was deleted
An orphan is always in the Orders table, a dangling reference is always in a different table
Dangling references can be detected with LEFT JOIN, orphans cannot
There is no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
questions.right: Exactly — the SQL to find both is identical (that's the point the lesson is making), but the story behind each one is different, and that story is what determines the correct fix.
