Zero-based month numbering is always invalid regardless of the source system's own internal conventions
This mismatch only affects the Quarter column, never a dedicated Month column, in any table
questions.right: Right — the mismatch between a zero-based source convention and SQL Server's one-based convention is exactly what produces off-by-one invalid month values during import.
questions.wrong: Some programming languages and systems represent January as month 0 and December as month 11 (zero-based), while SQL Server and standard calendar convention represent January as 1 and December as 12 (one-based). If data is imported from a zero-based source without adjusting the offset, every month value ends up shifted down by one — producing an invalid Month = 0 (which should have been January = 1) and potentially losing what should be month 12 (December) since the zero-based system's highest value would only reach 11.

questions.q: Why does the lesson prefer DATEPART(ISO_WEEK, ...) over plain DATEPART(WEEK, ...) for international systems needing consistent week numbering?
choices: DATEPART(WEEK, ...) depends on the session's @@DATEFIRST setting and can return inconsistent results depending on that configuration, while DATEPART(ISO_WEEK, ...) follows the fixed, internationally standardized ISO 8601 week numbering regardless of local server settings
DATEPART(ISO_WEEK, ...) is significantly faster to execute than DATEPART(WEEK, ...) for any given date
DATEPART(WEEK, ...) can only return values between 1 and 12, making it unsuitable for weekly data
ISO_WEEK and WEEK always return identical results in every SQL Server configuration, making the choice purely stylistic
questions.right: Right — DATEPART(WEEK,...) is sensitive to the same configurable @@DATEFIRST setting that affects weekday numbering, while ISO_WEEK follows a fixed international standard that doesn't shift with local configuration.
questions.wrong: Just as DATEPART(WEEKDAY, ...) is affected by @@DATEFIRST, DATEPART(WEEK, ...) is similarly influenced by that same configurable setting, meaning it can return different week numbers for the same date depending on server/session configuration. DATEPART(ISO_WEEK, ...) instead follows the ISO 8601 international standard consistently, which doesn't shift based on local settings — making it the more reliable and portable choice for systems that need to agree on week numbers across different environments or countries.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe an off-by-one import error affecting Quarter values (like the batch of 847 records with an invalid Quarter = 0) as capable of distorting an entire seasonal analysis, rather than just being a handful of odd rows?
choices: Because the error was systematic (affecting an entire batch, not isolated rows) and the invalid Quarter value causes those records to be silently excluded by any query using WHERE Quarter BETWEEN 1 AND 4, the affected quarter's reported totals can appear near-zero even though the underlying data actually exists
Invalid Quarter values are automatically corrected by SQL Server before any aggregate function processes them
A Quarter value of 0 causes the entire query to fail with a runtime error rather than silently excluding rows
Off-by-one import errors can only ever affect a single row at a time, never an entire import batch
questions.right: Right — because the error hit an entire import batch systematically, and standard range-based queries silently exclude the invalid values rather than erroring, the specific quarter's totals can look artificially near-zero rather than obviously broken.
questions.wrong: The scenario describes 847 records with the same systematic Quarter mapping error, not isolated one-off mistakes. Because WHERE Quarter BETWEEN 1 AND 4 silently excludes rows with Quarter = 0 (no error is raised, they just vanish from the result set), an entire quarter's worth of genuine data effectively disappears from any report built on that filter — making Q4 performance look near-zero when the real data is actually present in the table, just tagged with an invalid period value that standard queries don't recognize.

G05-T20.close: Invalid period numbers often trace back to zero-based versus one-based encoding mismatches during import, and their silent exclusion from range-filtered queries can make an entire reporting period look empty when the data actually exists, just mistagged.

G05-T21.open: The last lesson of Group 5 — using the population's own distribution, not a hardcoded number, to catch anomalies a stale fixed threshold would miss.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's opening scenario emphasize that a hardcoded '> 5%' threshold in an Excel dashboard failed to catch a branch's default rate anomaly, even though the true statistical threshold (mean + 3σ) would have caught it three months earlier?
choices: A fixed number stays frozen even as the underlying population's normal range shifts over time — a dynamic threshold recalculated from the population's own current mean and standard deviation adapts automatically, catching anomalies that a stale fixed number, set years ago and never revisited, would miss
The '> 5%' threshold was actually mathematically identical to mean + 3σ for this dataset, so the comparison in the scenario is misleading
Excel dashboards are structurally incapable of ever displaying a value above 5%, which is why the anomaly wasn't caught
The regulator only uses fixed thresholds, never statistical ones, making the internal threshold irrelevant to external detection
questions.right: Right — a fixed number set once and never revisited doesn't track how the population's normal range may shift, while a threshold recalculated from the population's own current mean and stddev adapts automatically.
questions.wrong: The scenario states the branch's 6.8% default rate was more than eleven standard deviations above the historical mean of 2.1% — a genuinely extreme statistical outlier. But the dashboard's hardcoded '> 5%' threshold, set years earlier and never updated, happened to sit in a range that didn't trigger until the rate had already climbed well past where a dynamic mean + 3σ threshold would have caught it. A threshold recalculated from the population's own current statistics adapts as that population's normal range evolves; a number typed into a spreadsheet years ago does not.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use NULLIF(StdDevTarget, 0) when calculating each Z-score, and specifically why NULLIF rather than just checking StdDevTarget > 0 in a WHERE clause?
choices: NULLIF converts a StdDevTarget of exactly 0 into NULL right inside the division itself, which makes the division return NULL instead of raising a divide-by-zero runtime error — this keeps the row present in the result set with a NULL Z-score, rather than needing to filter the row out entirely beforehand
NULLIF and a WHERE StdDevTarget > 0 filter are functionally interchangeable and produce exactly the same result set in every case
NULLIF is required syntax any time STDEV() appears anywhere in a T-SQL query
A StdDevTarget of 0 can never actually occur in real SalesTargets data, so this is purely defensive coding with no real purpose
questions.right: Right — NULLIF turns the problematic 0 into NULL right at the division, avoiding an error while still letting the row appear in the output (with a NULL Z-score) rather than being filtered out entirely.
questions.wrong: If a group has only one record, or all records in a group happen to have identical TargetAmount values, STDEV() returns 0. Dividing by 0 directly would raise a runtime error. NULLIF(StdDevTarget, 0) converts that specific 0 into NULL, and since SQL Server division by NULL returns NULL (not an error), the row still appears in the result set — just with a NULL ZScore rather than a computed value — which is different from filtering the row out of the result entirely with a WHERE clause.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend percentile-based bands (P10-P90) as a non-parametric alternative to Z-score for identifying outliers, specifically for skewed financial data?
choices: Percentile calculations are based on the actual rank-ordering of the data rather than the mean and standard deviation, so they aren't distorted by extreme values the way Z-score's own inputs (mean, stddev) can be pulled off-center by the very outliers being searched for
Percentile-based detection always produces results identical to Z-score detection for any dataset, making the choice purely a matter of preference
PERCENTILE_CONT() cannot be computed using a window function and requires a separate query for each row
Percentile bands only work correctly on datasets with fewer than 50 total rows
questions.right: Exactly — percentile bands are computed from rank-order position, not from the mean/stddev that outliers themselves can distort, making them a more robust choice for skewed data.
questions.wrong: Z-score depends on the mean and standard deviation of the very data being examined — and in a skewed distribution, a few extreme values can meaningfully shift both the mean and standard deviation, distorting the baseline used to judge what counts as 'unusual.' Percentile-based measures (like P10 and P90) are computed from the rank-ordered position of values within the distribution, which is inherently more resistant to being skewed by a small number of extreme outliers — making them the more robust ('non-parametric') choice when the underlying distribution isn't close to normal.

G05-T21.close: That completes Group 5 — Range/Boundary, 21 lessons. Every lesson circled the same core question from a different angle: is this value, or this derived value, inside the bounds it should be in — and is the threshold itself still the right one to measure against?

G06-T01.open: This lesson starts Group 6 by checking whether two columns that describe the same real-world fact can contradict each other. The key move is to reason from the stored status and the date column together, not either field in isolation.

questions.q: In this lesson, what is the core consistency rule for Employees using IsActive and TerminationDate?
choices: A terminated employee must have IsActive = 0 and a TerminationDate, while an active employee must have IsActive = 1 and no TerminationDate
Any employee with a TerminationDate must always be deleted from the table
IsActive alone is sufficient, so TerminationDate can be ignored
TerminationDate is only for reporting and never affects access control
questions.right: That is the lesson's rule: both columns encode the same fact and must agree.
questions.wrong: The lesson treats this as a logical contradiction between two columns, not a deletion rule or a one-column-only check. It also shows why access-control logic can be wrong if IsActive and TerminationDate drift apart.

questions.q: Why does the solution use a CASE expression instead of a simple NOT NULL check?
choices: Because the query needs to classify multiple column combinations, not just detect a missing value
Because NOT NULL cannot be used in SQL Server
Because CASE is required whenever GETDATE() appears
Because NOT NULL only works on string columns
questions.right: CASE lets the query name each contradiction pattern, such as a termination date paired with an active-looking row.
questions.wrong: A NOT NULL check only finds missing data in one column. The lesson needs to evaluate combinations of values and explain whether each combination is contradictory or merely incomplete.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about a delivered order that has no DeliveryDate versus a pending order that has no delivery date?
choices: The first is a contradiction, while the second is incompleteness rather than contradiction
Both are the same type of contradiction
Both are harmless because the status column is enough
Only the pending order is a contradiction
questions.right: The lesson explicitly separates contradiction from incompleteness, and only the status/date mismatch is a contradiction.
questions.wrong: The lesson distinguishes a status/date conflict from a missing-but-not-conflicting value. A delivered order without a date says two things at once that cannot both be true, while a pending order with no date may simply be unfinished.

G06-T01.close: Next lessons in Group 6 keep the same idea: a row is wrong when its fields disagree in a way that breaks business meaning. The checks just get broader, moving from one row to many rows and across tables.

G06-T02.open: This lesson expands consistency checks from one row to two tables. The important distinction is between an intentional historical snapshot and an accidental stale copy, because only one of those is a true mismatch.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend joining Orders to Customers for the current email instead of trusting Orders.Email?
choices: Because Orders.Email may be a stale copy that does not update when the customer changes their email
Because Orders cannot store any customer-related data
Because Customers never changes, so it is always the faster table
Because joining to Customers removes the need for any consistency checks
questions.right: The lesson's point is that denormalised copies become stale when the master record changes.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not saying customer data cannot exist in Orders at all. It is saying that if the same fact is duplicated, the copy can drift unless there is an explicit reason for it to differ.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by a point-in-time snapshot?
choices: A copied value that is allowed to differ from the master because it captures the value at the time of the event
A value that is always wrong if it differs from the parent table
A value that can only be stored in a temporary table
A value that must be recomputed every time the row is read
questions.right: The lesson explicitly warns that some cross-table differences are intentional, especially historical snapshots such as order-time prices.
questions.wrong: The lesson says not every difference is an error. Some values, like an order's price at sale time, are meant to preserve history even if the master table has changed since then.

questions.q: Why does Step 2 compare Orders.TotalAmount to SUM(Transactions.Amount)?
choices: To perform a reconciliation check that catches missed transactions or amount mismatches
To prove that every order must have exactly one transaction
To replace the Orders table with the Transactions table
To validate currency codes
questions.right: That is the reconciliation pattern the lesson teaches: a header total should match the detail rows within a tolerance.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses the aggregate comparison as a consistency check, not as a uniqueness rule or a schema replacement. It is meant to catch amounts that no longer reconcile.

G06-T02.close: The next lesson keeps the same consistency theme but shifts from stored copies to recomputed values. Instead of asking whether two tables agree, it asks whether a stored total still matches what the source data implies.

G06-T03.open: This lesson is about derived values going stale. The key idea is that a stored total, commission, or hash is only trustworthy if it still matches what you get when you recompute it from the source columns.

questions.q: What is the main reason the lesson gives for a derived value becoming stale?
choices: A source column changes but the stored total is not recalculated
SQL Server automatically deletes derived values after six months
Derived values only work for integers
The value is always stale if it uses ROUND
questions.right: The lesson says drift happens when the source changes and the application or migration fails to recalculate the stored copy.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not frame staleness as an automatic time-based failure or a rounding problem. It is about change without synchronized recomputation.

questions.q: Why does the query allow a small difference such as less than 0.01?
choices: To tolerate penny-level rounding differences in financial comparisons
Because SQL Server cannot compare decimals exactly
Because any non-zero difference is ignored in this lesson
Because differences under 1.00 are considered invalid
questions.right: The lesson explicitly uses a penny tolerance to avoid false positives from minor rounding differences.
questions.wrong: The lesson still treats meaningful differences as mismatches. The small threshold is there only to avoid flagging harmless rounding noise.

questions.q: What architectural fix does the lesson recommend for stale derived values?
choices: Use a computed column or a view so the value is recalculated from the source data
Store more copies of the total in additional tables
Remove the source columns and keep only the derived value
Convert all amounts to strings before storing them
questions.right: The lesson says to eliminate the manual sync problem by deriving the value on read or via a persisted computed column that recalculates automatically.
questions.wrong: The lesson's fix is the opposite of storing more redundant copies. It recommends reducing drift by deriving the value from the source rather than duplicating it manually.

G06-T03.close: This lesson is the bridge from cross-table agreement to internal recalculation checks. The same consistency logic keeps showing up, but now the comparison is stored value versus recomputed value instead of one row versus another table.

G06-T04.open: This lesson changes the consistency problem from matching values to matching units. A number is not safely aggregatable unless you know what unit it is in, and the lesson makes that visible with currency.

questions.q: Why is SUM(Amount) across all transactions unsafe in the lesson's scenario?
choices: Because the amounts are in multiple currencies that cannot be added meaningfully without conversion
Because SUM cannot be used with numeric columns in SQL Server
Because the table contains no OrderID column
Because currency values are always stored as text
questions.right: The lesson's point is that GBP, EUR, and USD are different units, so a raw sum is meaningless without conversion or grouping.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not claim SUM is invalid for numeric columns. It says the operation is invalid when the values are in different units and are treated as if they were the same.

questions.q: What is the correct pattern for currency-safe aggregation in the lesson?
choices: Group by Currency, or convert everything to one currency before summing
Ignore Currency because totals are all that matter
Convert all amounts to strings so they display clearly
Use MAX(Amount) instead of SUM(Amount)
questions.right: The lesson explicitly says to segregate by unit first or convert via exchange rates before aggregating.
questions.wrong: The lesson is careful that the grouping key must be the unit column, or else a conversion table must be used. Simply ignoring the unit creates the exact error the lesson warns against.

questions.q: What does the lesson say Step 6 is trying to catch?
choices: Amounts that are implausible for the stated currency, such as a GBP amount that looks like a pence/pounds mix-up
Orders with duplicate ProductID values
Customers whose country code is missing
Transactions that are older than 90 days
questions.right: Step 6 is a plausibility check for magnitude errors, like values that suggest the wrong unit within a single currency.
questions.wrong: The lesson's Step 6 is not about lookup codes or date sequencing. It checks whether the numeric size makes sense for the currency context, which can expose pence-versus-pounds mistakes.

G06-T04.close: The next lessons stay in consistency territory but move into hierarchy and time. Here the central lesson is simple: do not aggregate values unless the unit is known and consistent.

G06-T05.open: This lesson takes consistency into recursive structures. The issue is no longer two columns disagreeing, but a self-referencing hierarchy that can loop forever if a node becomes its own ancestor.

questions.q: What does the lesson use to detect a direct self-reference in Employees?
choices: WHERE ManagerID = EmployeeID
WHERE ManagerID IS NULL
GROUP BY ManagerID HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY EmployeeID
questions.right: The lesson treats ManagerID = EmployeeID as the simplest cycle and checks it directly.
questions.wrong: The lesson's direct self-reference check is a single-row comparison. NULL managers identify roots, not self-managing employees.

questions.q: Why does the recursive CTE track AncestorPath as a string?
choices: To detect whether the current EmployeeID already appears in the path and therefore a cycle exists
To sort employees alphabetically
To avoid needing a ManagerID column
To replace MAXRECURSION completely
questions.right: The lesson uses CHARINDEX against the accumulated path to spot when a node reappears in its own ancestry.
questions.wrong: The path is not for sorting or replacing the hierarchy columns. It is a cycle-detection aid so the query can tell when recursion has looped back on itself.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Depth < 20 guard and MAXRECURSION?
choices: To prevent runaway recursion when a cycle exists
To make the query run faster on all hierarchies
To ensure every employee has exactly 20 managers
To force the root to appear last
questions.right: The lesson says recursive hierarchy checks need a safety limit so a bad cycle does not recurse indefinitely.
questions.wrong: The depth guard is not a business rule about the number of managers. It is a protection against infinite traversal when the data contains a cycle.

G06-T05.close: The next lesson shifts from structural loops to event order. Both problems are about invalid relationships, but here the relationship is chronological rather than hierarchical.

G06-T06.open: This lesson is about chronological order. The important habit is to check adjacent events in the expected chain and to read negative DATEDIFF results as an inverted sequence.

questions.q: What does a negative DATEDIFF(DAY, OrderDate, DeliveryDate) indicate in the lesson?
choices: DeliveryDate occurs before OrderDate, so the sequence is inverted
The order was delivered exactly on time
The order date is missing
DATEDIFF cannot be used on dates
questions.right: The lesson uses negative DATEDIFF as the visible sign that the later event happened before the earlier one.
questions.wrong: The lesson treats negative days as the hallmark of a sequence violation. A zero result is same-day and positive is the expected direction.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use LAG(DeliveryDate) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY OrderDate)?
choices: To compare each order with the previous delivery for the same customer and detect overlaps
To delete duplicate orders
To calculate currency conversions
To find the newest customer record
questions.right: The lesson uses LAG to look back at the previous row in the customer's order sequence and see if the next order arrived before the prior one was delivered.
questions.wrong: LAG here is not for deduplication or lookups. It is specifically to compare the current order against the previous order's delivery date.

questions.q: What root cause does the lesson mention for out-of-order timestamps across systems?
choices: Timezone conversion errors when timestamps are not normalised to a single timezone
Missing foreign keys between Orders and Transactions
Discounts entered as percentages instead of decimals
Case-sensitive collations
questions.right: The lesson explicitly calls out timezone normalisation as the source of impossible event order.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not tie sequence problems to keys, percentages, or collations. It points to timestamps coming from multiple systems without a common timezone.

G06-T06.close: The next lesson moves one level up from temporal order to grain and fan-out. It is still about consistency, but now the trap is adding together values that live at different aggregation levels.

G06-T07.open: This lesson shows how inconsistency appears when you mix row-level detail with pre-aggregated values. The central risk is fan-out: a parent row gets repeated for every child row and then summed multiple times.

questions.q: Why is SUM(Orders.TotalAmount) after joining to Transactions called a fan-out error in the lesson?
choices: Because each order total is repeated once per matching transaction and gets counted multiple times
Because SUM only works on distinct values
Because fan-out is the same thing as a missing foreign key
Because Orders rows are deleted during the join
questions.right: The lesson explains that the parent row is multiplied by child rows, so the same order total is summed repeatedly.
questions.wrong: The error is not about SUM itself or missing keys. It is about the join changing the grain and causing the parent amount to be counted once per transaction.

questions.q: What is the lesson's recommended fix for the fan-out problem?
choices: Aggregate the child table to the parent grain first, then join
Use DISTINCT on the final result only
Join all tables first and fix the count with ROUND
Replace JOIN with UNION
questions.right: The lesson's fix is to produce one row per order in the child aggregate before joining it to Orders.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not recommend hiding the fan-out with DISTINCT or rounding. It says the grain must be aligned before the join.

questions.q: What does Step 4's monthly reconciliation test?
choices: Whether monthly Order totals and monthly Transaction totals match
Whether every customer has exactly one order per month
Whether all products are active
Whether transactions use the same currency
questions.right: The lesson uses a monthly roll-up to compare two aggregated views of the same business activity.
questions.wrong: The monthly query is a reconciliation check, not a uniqueness or product-status check. It compares totals at the same grain to find gaps.

G06-T07.close: The next lesson returns to row-level business rules, but now the rule is conditional: one field changes whether another field is required or forbidden. That is a different kind of consistency than grain alignment.

G06-T08.open: This lesson focuses on conditional dependencies, where one field's value determines whether another field must exist or must not exist. The main skill is turning an implication into a SQL CASE or CHECK rule.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by a conditional dependency?
choices: A rule where field A's value determines whether field B is required, forbidden, or constrained
A rule that every table must have a primary key
A rule that only dates can be NULL
A rule that all columns must use the same datatype
questions.right: That is the lesson's definition: the value of one column controls what is allowed in another.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not about keys or datatypes. It is about business rules such as Delivered implying DeliveryDate is present.

questions.q: Why can't the rule 'Delivered orders must have DeliveryDate' be enforced by a simple column-level NOT NULL constraint?
choices: Because the field is only required when Status has a specific value
Because SQL Server does not support NOT NULL
Because DeliveryDate must always be NULL
Because NOT NULL only works on computed columns
questions.right: The lesson explains that the requirement is conditional on Status, so a table-level rule is needed instead of an unconditional column rule.
questions.wrong: The issue is not that NOT NULL is unavailable. The issue is that the requirement is contextual, so a single unconditional constraint cannot express it.

questions.q: Which combination is explicitly flagged in the lesson's Orders check?
choices: Cancelled with DeliveryDate not NULL
Delivered with DeliveryDate not NULL
Pending with DeliveryDate NULL
Shipped with DeliveryDate NULL
questions.right: The lesson marks Cancelled with a non-NULL DeliveryDate as a violation, along with Delivered missing a date and Pending having one.
questions.wrong: The lesson's violation list includes Cancelled orders that still have a delivery date. Pending with NULL is not a violation there, and Delivered with a non-NULL date is not what the rule forbids.

G06-T08.close: The next lesson moves from conditional dependencies to value lists and code domains. The theme stays the same: a field is only valid when its value fits the business rule attached to it.

G06-T09.open: This lesson is about sign consistency. The row may look numerically valid on its own, but the sign has to mean the right business thing or every balance calculation is wrong.

questions.q: What is the main sign rule in this lesson for Transactions.Amount?
choices: Negative amounts are a violation when the business rule requires positive values
All amounts must be stored as text
Positive amounts are invalid for refunds
The sign does not matter if the total is correct
questions.right: The lesson explicitly flags negative transaction amounts when the business expects positive values.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not saying sign is optional. It says the business meaning of sign must be consistent, or balances and totals become wrong.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn about SUM(Amount) even when every individual amount looks plausible?
choices: Because if sign convention is wrong, the same SUM can produce gross or net totals with very different meanings
Because SUM only works for negative values
Because Amount should never be aggregated
Because a zero-value transaction always cancels the query
questions.right: The lesson's point is that the same-looking SUM can either net debits and credits or just add everything up, depending on sign convention.
questions.wrong: The issue is not that aggregation is forbidden. It is that the meaning of the sum changes completely depending on whether the values are signed or unsigned.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about zero-value transactions?
choices: They are often errors or test entries, though some legitimate cases exist
They are always valid and should never be checked
They prove the sign convention is correct
They are only relevant to currency conversion
questions.right: The lesson treats zero as suspicious because it can indicate a processing error, while acknowledging that a legitimate zero can exist.
questions.wrong: The lesson is careful not to declare every zero wrong. It says zero amounts often deserve review because they can distort averages and signal bad data.

G06-T09.close: The next lesson moves from sign to controlled vocabularies. It is still a consistency problem, but now the question is whether a stored code actually belongs to the allowed reference set.

G06-T10.open: This lesson validates lookup codes against a reference set. The important distinction is between a truly invalid code and a variant encoding of a valid code, because those need different fixes.

questions.q: What SQL pattern does the lesson use to find codes that are not in the reference table?
choices: A LEFT JOIN to the reference table with WHERE reference.code IS NULL
A CROSS JOIN to every possible code
A UNION of all valid and invalid codes
A window function over the code column
questions.right: The lesson uses the anti-join pattern to surface stored values that have no matching reference row.
questions.wrong: The lesson is specifically about anti-joins, not cross joins or unions. A missing match in the reference table is what flags the code as invalid.

questions.q: How does the lesson distinguish a variant encoding from a truly invalid code?
choices: By mapping common aliases like UK to the ISO code GB
By deleting all codes that do not match exactly
By converting all codes to lowercase
By treating every unknown code as valid
questions.right: The lesson shows that some codes are aliases or non-standard variants that can be mapped to a canonical value.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not say all unknown codes are acceptable. It separates aliases that can be corrected from values that need investigation.

questions.q: Why are lookup mismatches especially dangerous according to the lesson?
choices: Because affected records become invisible to standard filters such as WHERE Country = 'GB'
Because SQL Server refuses to store them
Because they automatically fix themselves
Because they only affect sorting, not filtering
questions.right: The lesson says the records still exist, but queries filtering on the expected code miss them, so counts and reports are understated.
questions.wrong: The problem is not storage or sorting. The problem is that reports using the correct filter value will not see rows stored with the wrong code.

G06-T10.close: The next lesson returns to multi-row logic. Instead of checking whether a code belongs to a set, it checks whether a business rule about the number of rows per key has been broken.

G06-T11.open: This lesson is about multi-row constraints, where a business rule depends on how many rows share the same key. The SQL pattern is GROUP BY plus HAVING, and the lesson also shows how to expose the exact duplicate rows.

questions.q: What does HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 detect in the lesson?
choices: A key combination that should be unique but appears more than once
A row with a NULL value
A transaction that is negative
A status transition that is invalid
questions.right: The lesson uses GROUP BY to define the rule key and HAVING to keep only groups with duplicate rows.
questions.wrong: The query is not checking NULLs, signs, or state transitions. It is checking whether a supposed unique combination appears more than once.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use ROW_NUMBER() over the duplicate groups?
choices: To identify which row is the canonical one and which rows are duplicates
To calculate currency totals
To force SQL Server to sort the table physically
To replace the GROUP BY
questions.right: The lesson says row numbering helps decide which duplicate to keep and which ones to remove or merge.
questions.wrong: ROW_NUMBER is not being used as a replacement for aggregation. It is used after duplicates are found so each row in the duplicate group can be distinguished.

questions.q: What is the effect of duplicate SalesTargets rows in the lesson's example?
choices: The target total becomes inflated, which can distort commission calculations
The rows are automatically merged by SQL Server
The duplicate rows do not matter because SUM ignores them
The employee becomes inactive
questions.right: The lesson shows that duplicates inflate the target denominator and can make performance appear worse than it is.
questions.wrong: The lesson is explicit that duplicate rows are dangerous because aggregations will include them. SQL Server does not automatically merge them away.

G06-T11.close: The next lesson moves from multi-row counts to allowed status changes. The row count is not the issue anymore; the issue is whether the current state could have come from a valid prior state.

G06-T12.open: This lesson treats status as a state machine. The key idea is that a status is only valid if it can be reached through a permitted transition from the previous state.

questions.q: What is the lesson's main limitation when only the current Status is stored in Orders?
choices: It cannot fully prove transition history, so some previous-state inference is approximate
It cannot filter by Status at all
It forces every order to be Pending
It means DeliveryDate must be NULL
questions.right: The lesson says you can infer likely previous states, but without a history table you cannot fully prove how the record got there.
questions.wrong: The limitation is not about filtering or forcing a single status. It is about not having explicit transition history, which makes full validation incomplete.

questions.q: Which transitions are considered terminal in the lesson?
choices: Delivered and Cancelled
Pending and Processing
Processing and Shipped
Any status with a DeliveryDate
questions.right: The lesson explicitly labels Delivered and Cancelled as terminal states with no further transitions allowed.
questions.wrong: Pending and Processing are active states in the lesson, not terminal ones. Terminal states are the endpoints of the workflow.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say CHECK constraints alone are not enough for transition validation?
choices: Because transition rules depend on the previous value, not just the current column value
Because CHECK constraints cannot use any columns
Because transition rules only apply to dates
Because CHECK constraints delete invalid rows automatically
questions.right: A transition rule needs old state plus new state, which is why the lesson points to triggers or application-layer validation instead of a simple CHECK.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not saying CHECK is impossible in general. It is saying it cannot capture the prior-to-current-state relationship needed for a state machine.

G06-T12.close: The next lesson returns to parent-child agreement. Instead of asking how a row got into its current state, it asks whether a child record still agrees with the parent record it depends on.

G06-T13.open: This lesson is about denormalised child attributes that must agree with the parent. The core check is simple: if a child repeats a parent property, the two values need to match unless a business exception is documented.

questions.q: What does the lesson check first with Orders and Products?
choices: Whether an order references an inactive product
Whether product prices are always positive
Whether every order has exactly one product
Whether products have matching VAT rates
questions.right: The lesson flags orders that point to a product whose current status is inactive or missing.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not doing a price positivity check there. It is checking whether the order is linked to a product that should no longer be used.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use a LEFT JOIN for the parent-child check?
choices: To catch both mismatched parents and orphan rows where the parent is missing
To sort the results alphabetically
To avoid checking inactive products
To guarantee only one row per order
questions.right: The lesson explains that a LEFT JOIN lets you detect missing parent rows as well as mismatched values.
questions.wrong: The join type is about visibility of orphaned rows, not sorting or deduplication. A LEFT JOIN preserves the child so the missing parent can be seen.

questions.q: What nuance does the lesson mention about employee department versus manager department?
choices: Cross-department reporting lines can be legitimate and should be reviewed rather than blindly rejected
Every department mismatch must be deleted immediately
Department values are never compared to managers
Only inactive employees can have mismatches
questions.right: The lesson notes that some mismatches are valid exceptions, so the query flags them for review instead of declaring every one a hard error.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not assume every department mismatch is impossible. It deliberately leaves room for legitimate cross-department reporting relationships.

G06-T13.close: The next lesson turns from agreement between parent and child to how many children are allowed. The question becomes one of cardinality rather than attribute match.

G06-T14.open: This lesson is about cardinality rules: minimums, maximums, and exact counts. The same pattern is used to find missing child rows, too many child rows, and overloaded managers.

questions.q: What does NOT EXISTS detect in the lesson's Orders check?
choices: Orders with no transactions, violating the minimum cardinality of 1
Orders with too many products
Orders that are cancelled
Transactions that are negative
questions.right: The lesson uses NOT EXISTS to find parent rows with zero children when at least one is required.
questions.wrong: The query is not about products, cancellation, or signs. It is specifically checking for the absence of any matching transaction rows.

questions.q: How does the lesson detect a maximum cardinality violation of more than 3 transactions per order?
choices: GROUP BY OrderID HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
WHERE TransactionCount = 3
ORDER BY TransactionDate DESC
LAG(TransactionID) OVER (...)
questions.right: The lesson uses GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 to isolate orders that exceed the permitted child count.
questions.wrong: The violation is not found by sorting or by exact equality to 3. It is found by grouping each order's transactions and filtering groups that exceed the threshold.

questions.q: What does Step 4 apply cardinality to besides orders?
choices: Managers with too many direct reports
Products with too many categories
Customers with too many emails
Transactions with too many currencies
questions.right: The lesson extends the same concept to span of control, flagging managers with more than the allowed number of direct reports.
questions.wrong: The step is about the management hierarchy, not product categories or codes. It counts direct reports per manager and compares that to the business limit.

G06-T14.close: The next lesson is another form of business orphaning, but this time caused by soft deletes. The FK may still exist technically, while the business relationship is already broken.

G06-T15.open: This lesson covers soft-delete cascades. The key insight is that a child can be an orphan in business terms even when the foreign key still points to a valid parent row.

questions.q: What is the main issue when Customers.IsActive is set to 0 but open orders remain active?
choices: The orders become business-level orphans and may still be processed when they should be stopped
The database automatically deletes the orders
The customer row becomes a foreign key error
The orders can no longer be joined to Customers
questions.right: The lesson says the relationship still exists technically, but the business rule has been violated because active processing continues for a deactivated customer.
questions.wrong: The issue is not a broken FK or automatic deletion. The problem is that the parent is inactive while the child still behaves as if the relationship were active.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say standard FK constraints do not catch this problem?
choices: Because the parent row still exists, so referential integrity is technically satisfied
Because FK constraints only work on text columns
Because Orders cannot reference Customers
Because soft deletes are always unsupported
questions.right: The lesson explains that a soft-deleted parent is still physically present, so the FK remains valid even though the business meaning is wrong.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not claim soft deletes are unsupported. It says the problem is logical rather than referential, so FK constraints alone will not detect it.

questions.q: What remediation does the lesson recommend?
choices: Update the customer and cancel dependent orders in the same transaction
Leave the orders active and rely on reports
Hard-delete all historical rows
Change the FK to nullable
questions.right: The lesson emphasizes atomic deactivation plus cancellation so the state change cannot be half-applied.
questions.wrong: The lesson's fix is not to loosen integrity or discard history. It is to cascade the business action in one transaction so the active children do not survive the parent's deactivation.

G06-T15.close: The final lesson in this set deals with strings rather than business state. It checks whether values that should compare the same are being stored in incompatible case or accent variants.

G06-T16.open: This lesson is about encoding and collation consistency. The same logical value can look different on disk because of case or accent differences, and the lesson shows how that affects matching and deduplication.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use LOWER(Email) when finding duplicate email addresses?
choices: To compare emails case-insensitively and detect logical duplicates stored with different case
To encrypt the email address
To make the email column numeric
To force duplicates to disappear automatically
questions.right: The lesson says LOWER() is a simple way to normalize case for comparison so logically identical emails can be matched.
questions.wrong: The function is not for encryption or cleanup. It is for comparison, and the lesson also notes the tradeoff that wrapping in LOWER() can reduce index usage.

questions.q: What does COLLATE Latin1_General_CS_AS do in the lesson's email comparison?
choices: Forces a case-sensitive comparison on a case-insensitive database
Deletes accents from the text
Converts the column to lowercase
Makes all comparisons binary
questions.right: The lesson uses COLLATE to prove the stored values differ in case even if the database default collation would treat them as equal.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not using COLLATE to strip accents or change storage. It is explicitly controlling comparison sensitivity for that expression.

questions.q: What is the recommended fix for mixed-case values that are meant to be the same logical value?
choices: Normalize to a canonical form at ingest, such as lowercase emails or uppercase product codes
Store both case variants forever
Rely on DISTINCT in every query
Change all values to NULL
questions.right: The lesson says the right fix is canonical normalization during data entry or ETL, not repeated ad hoc comparison logic.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not recommend preserving all variants or hiding them with DISTINCT. It recommends preventing the inconsistency at ingest so downstream queries stay simple and reliable.

G06-T16.close: That completes the 16 consistency lessons. Across them, the common thread is that SQL validation is usually about making an implicit business rule explicit, then checking whether the stored data actually obeys it.

G07-T01.open: Start with the business-rule framing from Group 7: this lesson treats minimum order value as a post-check validation, not a data type issue. The key pattern is separating zero, negative, token, and sub-minimum positive orders before looking at aggregate revenue impact.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat a £0.50 order differently from a £0.00 order in the violation label?
choices: Because £0.50 is a valid positive amount but still breaches the minimum order value, while £0.00 is classified as a free order
Because both are invalid currency values and must be rejected by the data type
Because £0.00 always means a refund and £0.50 always means a chargeback
Because the query groups all amounts below £10 into one label
questions.right: That matches the lesson’s CASE logic: zero-value orders are labelled separately from token and sub-minimum positive orders.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly distinguishes zero, negative, token, and below-minimum positive amounts. £0.50 is not a data type error; it is a positive order that still violates the business threshold.

questions.q: What is Step 3 calculating when it uses `COUNT(*) * @MinOrderValue - SUM(TotalAmount)`?
choices: The revenue lost if all sub-minimum positive orders had been raised to the minimum threshold
The number of cancelled orders that were refunded
The average order value across all customers
The fulfilment cost per order
questions.right: Exactly. The query compares actual revenue to the revenue that would have been earned at the minimum order value.
questions.wrong: Step 3 is a revenue-impact calculation, not a refund, average, or fulfilment-cost query. It shows the gap between actual sub-minimum revenue and the minimum allowed revenue.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 use `ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY YEAR(OrderDate)), 1)`?
choices: To show the share of each year's sub-minimum orders that falls in each month
To calculate the monthly average order value for each customer
To compare each month's revenue against the entire table total
To convert pounds into pence before grouping
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses the windowed total per year so each month can be shown as a percentage of that year’s sub-minimum orders.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s explanation is about seasonal patterns within each year. The `PARTITION BY YEAR(OrderDate)` window makes the denominator the yearly sub-minimum count, not a customer average or a table-wide total.

G07-T01.close: That lesson moves from row-level violations to customer and revenue impact, which is the same detective pattern used throughout Business Rules. Next lessons keep that theme but apply it to exposure, eligibility, and control bypasses.

G07-T02.open: This lesson builds on the same business-rule idea, but the threshold is cumulative credit exposure rather than a single transaction value. The important shift is that the check must sum active orders first, then compare to the credit ceiling.

questions.q: What is the core credit-control rule the lesson says should be enforced?
choices: Sum outstanding orders for a customer and compare that total to the credit limit
Reject any order over £10,000 regardless of customer history
Allow credit as long as each individual order is below the limit
Only check delivered orders because they are the only ones that matter
questions.right: That is the lesson’s main point: credit checks must be cumulative, not per-order.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly says a per-transaction check is insufficient. Delivered and cancelled orders are excluded from the outstanding balance used for the credit check.

questions.q: Which order statuses does the lesson treat as part of outstanding exposure in the main query?
choices: Any status not in Delivered, Cancelled, or Refunded
Only Pending and Processing, because those are active states
Only Delivered, because fulfilled orders still count as exposure
Only Cancelled, because they are the only unpaid records
questions.right: Correct. The query excludes Delivered, Cancelled, and Refunded from the exposure calculation.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s CTE filters out delivered, cancelled, and refunded orders. It does not define exposure as only Pending/Processing, and it does not include delivered orders in the active balance here.

questions.q: Why does Step 2 compute `CurrentOutstanding + ProposedOrderAmount` before making a decision?
choices: To simulate a pre-order credit check and reject an order that would push the customer over limit
To recalculate the customer’s credit limit from historical orders
To find duplicate orders by amount
To decide whether the order should be marked as refunded
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses that projection to show how the system should stop a breach before the order is committed.
questions.wrong: Step 2 is about projected exposure, not credit-limit recomputation, duplicate detection, or refunds. It is a preventive check, not a reconciliation step.

G07-T02.close: The key pattern here is aggregation before validation, which is a recurring theme in the rest of Group 7. Next lessons vary the aggregation target: rates, dates, transactions, and authorisation controls.

G07-T03.open: This lesson stays in Group 7’s business-rule lane, but now the validation target is a rate field. The main gotcha is that a percentage column can be corrupted either by impossible values or by decimal-vs-percentage confusion.

questions.q: Why does the lesson flag `DiscountPercent = 0.10` as suspicious in Step 3?
choices: Because a tiny non-zero value may mean the API sent 10% as a decimal fraction instead of 10
Because any value under 1 is mathematically impossible for a percentage field
Because the column can only store integers
Because 0.10 always means a 10% surcharge
questions.right: Right. The lesson treats very small positive values as possible decimal-entry errors, especially when the business expects percentage notation.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not say values below 1 are impossible. It says they can be plausible but suspicious, because they may reflect a percentage/decimal mix-up.

questions.q: Which condition is checked before the lesson considers approval tiers like manager or director sign-off?
choices: Whether the discount is above 100%, below 0, or NULL
Whether the product price is above £50
Whether the salesperson is terminated
Whether the discount is exactly 10%
questions.right: Correct. The query first filters out NULL, negative, and over-30 values, then labels the band by severity.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s validation starts with range checks and only then classifies tiered approval bands. It is not based on product price, employment status, or an exact 10% threshold.

questions.q: What is the negative effective price example intended to show?
choices: A discount over 100% produces a negative sale value, which is financially catastrophic
A commission of 110% is a normal high-performing sales rate
A zero discount always makes the effective price negative
A rate over 30% is only a reporting issue, not a financial one
questions.right: Yes. The explanation says a discount above 100% yields a negative effective price, meaning the business would owe the customer money.
questions.wrong: The lesson treats a discount above 100% as impossible and dangerous, not as a normal or merely cosmetic value. The negative effective price is the key failure mode.

G07-T03.close: This lesson is mostly about catching impossible rates and plausible-looking entry errors before they propagate into pricing or commission calculations. The next lessons move from rate validity into date, stock, and transaction controls.

G07-T04.open: This lesson is about exact age checking, which is one of the clearest examples of a business rule that looks simple but fails if you use only the year. The query’s real lesson is the birthday adjustment on top of `DATEDIFF(YEAR, ...)`.

questions.q: Why is `YEAR(GETDATE()) - YEAR(DateOfBirth)` unsafe for age eligibility?
choices: It ignores whether the birthday has already occurred this year
It always returns a negative value for minors
It only works for leap-year birthdays
It cannot be used with dates stored in SQL Server
questions.right: Correct. The lesson shows that year-only logic can mark someone as 18 before their actual birthday has happened.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s issue is not sign or leap-year handling. It is that year-only subtraction crosses a calendar year boundary before the birthday is reached.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the CASE adjustment subtracted from `DATEDIFF(YEAR, DateOfBirth, GETDATE())`?
choices: To subtract one year when the birthday has not yet occurred this year
To convert age into months
To handle NULL DateOfBirth values automatically
To make every customer appear one year younger
questions.right: Yes. That is the standard exact-age correction the lesson explicitly teaches.
questions.wrong: The CASE expression is a birthday check, not a month conversion or NULL handler. It only subtracts one when the current date has not yet reached the birthday in the current year.

questions.q: What does Step 3’s `FALSE APPROVAL` label mean?
choices: Year-only age says 18 or over, but exact age is still under 18
The customer is exactly 18 on their birthday
The customer has no DateOfBirth stored
The customer is allowed to buy alcohol because they are close to 18
questions.right: That is the discrepancy the lesson wants you to detect: the simplified year-only method would wrongly approve the customer.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s discrepancy check is specifically about a false positive caused by year-only age logic. It is not about exact birthdays or missing DOBs.

G07-T04.close: The important takeaway is that legal age is completed years of life, not a year-number difference. The next lessons continue the same control mindset with duplicate detection, stock, and salary rules.

G07-T05.open: This lesson shifts from threshold validation to duplicate detection. The core reasoning is that duplicates are defined by the fields that should be unique together, and the lesson shows both exact and near-duplicate patterns.

questions.q: What makes the Step 1 duplicate check reliable in this lesson?
choices: It groups by the combination of OrderID, Amount, Currency, and the date part of TransactionDate
It groups only by Amount so repeated values are easy to spot
It compares each transaction to the customer’s total monthly spend
It flags any transaction that happens more than once anywhere in the table
questions.right: Correct. The lesson defines the uniqueness key as the combination of order, amount, currency, and date.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not use amount alone or a whole-table count. It groups by the combination that should uniquely identify the payment event.

questions.q: Why does Step 2 use `LAG(TransactionDate)`?
choices: To compare a transaction to the previous one for the same order and amount and measure suspiciously short gaps
To sort transactions by currency
To calculate the average amount per customer
To find refunds before purchases
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses `LAG` to find a previous row and then checks the minute gap between the two timestamps.
questions.wrong: `LAG` in this lesson is not about currency, averages, or refunds. It is used for sequential duplicate detection within the same order-and-amount partition.

questions.q: What does a duplicate `CorrelationID` indicate in Step 3?
choices: An idempotency violation or gateway/key reuse problem
A normal repeated customer name
A valid way to group all daily transactions
A refund that was processed correctly
questions.right: Correct. The lesson treats repeated correlation IDs as a duplicate-processing failure.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly says the correlation key should be unique if it is being used as an idempotency key. Repeated values are a duplicate-transaction signal, not a normal grouping mechanism.

G07-T05.close: This lesson is a good template for detective controls: exact-key grouping first, then near-duplicate timing checks, then key reuse checks. The next lesson applies a similar post-hoc detection mindset to stock oversell.

G07-T06.open: This lesson is about oversell detection after concurrency has already gone wrong. The useful distinction is between detection queries and real-time prevention, and the lesson is explicit that SQL here is the detector, not the lock manager.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use `COUNT(*)` as a proxy for ordered units?
choices: Because the current schema has no Quantity column on Orders
Because quantity is always equal to the product price
Because COUNT is the same as SUM(Quantity) in every schema
Because orders are never linked to products
questions.right: Exactly. The explanation says a real system would sum line quantities, but this schema only gives order rows.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not say COUNT equals quantity in general. It says the schema lacks a Quantity column, so COUNT is just a demonstration proxy.

questions.q: Which orders are excluded from the oversell count in Step 1?
choices: Cancelled and Refunded orders
Delivered and Shipped orders only
Only orders above £1000
Only orders placed by inactive customers
questions.right: Right. The lesson counts active commitments and excludes cancelled and refunded orders from the stock pressure calculation.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly filters out cancelled and refunded orders because those units should not count against available stock. It does not exclude delivered or shipped orders by default in that step.

questions.q: What is the lesson’s recommended prevention mechanism for real-time oversell?
choices: Pessimistic locking or optimistic concurrency with a stock version counter
A monthly summary report
A GROUP BY on product category only
A discount rate validation rule
questions.right: Yes. The explanation names locking or version-based concurrency control as the preventative architecture.
questions.wrong: The lesson is very clear that the SQL query is for detection after the fact. Monthly reports and unrelated validation rules do not prevent concurrent oversells.

G07-T06.close: The key pattern here is that post-hoc validation can expose damage, but it cannot replace transaction-safe write controls. The next lessons keep using similar detective logic, but on pay, tax, and duty controls.

G07-T07.open: This lesson moves from transaction integrity to compensation compliance. The core idea is to normalise hourly pay into a comparable basis, compare it to a band table, and then separately check the legal minimum wage floor.

questions.q: Why does the lesson annualise salary as `HourlyRate * 37 * 52`?
choices: To compare an hourly rate against annual salary bands using the organisation’s full-time working week
Because 37 hours is the legal minimum for all UK workers
To convert salary into a daily rate
To calculate overtime premium
questions.right: Correct. The annualisation step makes hourly pay comparable to annual pay frameworks.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses 37 hours as the organisation’s assumed working week, not as a legal minimum for all workers. The purpose is comparability, not overtime calculation.

questions.q: What does the LEFT JOIN to `@SalaryBands` help detect?
choices: Employees whose EmploymentType is missing from the band table as well as employees outside the band
Only employees paid above the band maximum
Only interns
Only terminated employees
questions.right: Yes. The lesson says the LEFT JOIN catches both out-of-band rates and unknown employment types.
questions.wrong: The LEFT JOIN is used as a broad compliance check, not just for high earners or a single employee category. It also catches missing band definitions.

questions.q: Why does Step 3 check National Minimum Wage separately from the internal salary band?
choices: Because NMW is an absolute legal floor that can override a seemingly valid internal band
Because NMW only applies to contractors
Because internal bands are always stricter than law
Because the lesson is only interested in payroll taxes
questions.right: Exactly. The explanation says an internal band below the legal floor is itself illegal.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s point is that internal policy cannot undercut the law. NMW is checked independently because it is an external legal minimum, not just a company preference.

G07-T07.close: This lesson shows how business-rule validation can combine policy bands with hard legal floors. The next lessons extend that idea into tax rates, role separation, and refund linkage checks.

G07-T08.open: This lesson is about discrete tax-rate validation rather than a simple range check. The important idea is that a plausible-looking rate can still be invalid if it is not in the approved set for the jurisdiction.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a range check like `BETWEEN 0 AND 100` is not enough for VAT?
choices: Because UK VAT uses a small approved set of discrete rates, not any value in the range
Because VAT rates can never be stored as decimals
Because all tax rates must be negative
Because range checks are only for dates
questions.right: Correct. The explanation says 17% looks plausible but is not one of the approved UK rates.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s issue is not decimal storage or date checking. It is that VAT validity depends on membership in an approved set, not just being numerically plausible.

questions.q: What does Step 2 assume about `TotalAmount` when it calculates VAT?
choices: That `TotalAmount` is tax-inclusive and net amount must be extracted from it
That `TotalAmount` is always pre-tax and VAT is added later
That `TotalAmount` is a quantity count
That VAT is always zero on orders
questions.right: Yes. The lesson explicitly treats the total as gross and derives net and VAT from it.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s formula is gross-to-net extraction. It is not based on quantity counts or a universal zero tax assumption.

questions.q: What does Step 5’s category-level consistency check help find?
choices: Mixed VAT rates inside the same product category, which may signal a legitimate exception or a data error
Products that have no price
Transactions with duplicate order IDs
Customers in non-approved countries
questions.right: Right. The lesson uses category consistency to surface possible mismatches or exceptions that need documentation.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s Step 5 is about product-category VAT consistency, not pricing, duplicate transactions, or geo-restrictions.

G07-T08.close: The tax lesson is a good reminder that validation sometimes means checking a value against a reference set, not just a numeric boundary. The next lessons shift from tax into audit controls like segregation of duties and orphan refunds.

G07-T09.open: This lesson focuses on segregation of duties, which is a control design problem rather than a data-format problem. The SQL examples show how to detect a single person appearing in multiple sensitive roles or reusing transactional identifiers in suspicious ways.

questions.q: What is the core SoD violation pattern the lesson is trying to detect?
choices: The same person appearing in conflicting roles within a transaction or control chain
Any employee with a high salary
Any transaction above £10,000
Any order with a missing customer
questions.right: Correct. The lesson defines SoD as one person controlling multiple high-risk steps that should be separated.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not about salary levels, order sizes, or missing customers. It is about overlapping roles and control points.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 treat one `CorrelationID` across multiple orders as a concern?
choices: Because a unique idempotency key should not span multiple orders
Because correlation IDs are meant to be reused indefinitely
Because one customer can never place multiple orders
Because the database should always collapse orders into a single row
questions.right: Yes. The lesson says correlation-key reuse may indicate abuse or a control failure.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly treats correlation IDs as transaction-specific identifiers. Reuse across multiple orders is the suspicious condition, not the intended one.

questions.q: What is the difference between preventive and detective controls in the explanation?
choices: Access control is preventive, while SQL validation is detective
SQL validation is preventive and access control is detective
Both are the same thing
Neither one matters if the audit is internal
questions.right: Exactly. The explanation says SQL can catch failures, but the root control is access management.
questions.wrong: The lesson distinguishes the two: access control prevents the issue, while SQL-based validation detects it after the fact. They are not interchangeable.

G07-T09.close: This lesson is a classic audit-control pattern: identify role overlaps, then summarize the indicators that may point to fraud or broken process design. The next lesson follows that same audit logic for refunds that have no valid source transaction.

G07-T10.open: This lesson is about orphan refunds and over-refunds, which are both forms of payment integrity failure. The key technique is to aggregate purchases and refunds separately, then anti-join or compare the totals.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use `WHERE Amount < 0` to identify refunds?
choices: Because the schema represents refunds as negative amounts
Because all negative amounts are automatically chargebacks
Because negative amounts are impossible and always errors
Because the order amount column is stored as text
questions.right: Correct. The explanation says negative amounts are the refund indicator in this single-table ledger design.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly uses negative amounts as the refund convention in this schema. It does not say every negative amount is automatically a chargeback or a text error.

questions.q: What does the LEFT JOIN in Step 2 detect?
choices: Refund groups with no matching purchase group for the same OrderID
Refunds that happen on weekends
Customers with high order volume
Duplicate products in the catalog
questions.right: Yes. The anti-join pattern isolates refunds that have no corresponding positive purchase total.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s join is not about time-of-week, customer volume, or catalog duplication. It is specifically looking for orphan refund groups.

questions.q: Why is a refund before its purchase date treated as impossible?
choices: Because the timeline shows the refund happened before the original purchase event
Because refunds are always processed in a different currency
Because the customer must be inactive
Because the query only looks at cancelled orders
questions.right: Correct. The lesson calls a refund preceding the purchase a temporal impossibility and a sign of clock or data error.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s timing check is about event order, not currency or customer status. A refund cannot logically occur before the purchase that created it.

G07-T10.close: This lesson is a good example of deriving integrity from cross-table totals and event timing. The next lesson moves from payment integrity to frequency and velocity patterns, which are often a fraud signal.

G07-T11.open: This lesson contrasts simple bucketed counts with rolling-window analysis. The main idea is that frequency alone matters, but the size of the time window determines whether you catch bursty abuse or miss it.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of the tumbling hourly bucket in Step 2?
choices: It can miss bursts that cross an hour boundary
It cannot count transactions at all
It only works for customers, not bank accounts
It always overcounts by one
questions.right: Exactly. The explanation says a burst can be split across two adjacent buckets and appear less severe than it is.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not say tumbling windows are unusable. It says they are fast and simple but can miss bursts that cross bucket boundaries.

questions.q: How does the rolling-window check in Step 3 work?
choices: It self-joins transactions to prior transactions within the last 60 minutes
It groups all transactions by month
It only counts transactions after midnight
It compares amounts to the product price
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses a self-join with `DATEADD(MINUTE, -60, ...)` to count the prior-hour history for each transaction.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s rolling window is a self-join, not a monthly aggregate or a price comparison. It looks back 60 minutes from each transaction.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 combine SourceIP and DistinctAccounts?
choices: To detect one source creating lots of activity across many different accounts
To calculate customer age
To validate VAT rates
To find refunds with no purchase
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says breadth plus volume is a stronger fraud signal than volume alone.
questions.wrong: Step 4 is a velocity/fraud check, not an age, tax, or refund rule. The combination of IP and distinct accounts is the key signal.

G07-T11.close: This lesson shows both operational fraud monitoring and the tradeoff between simplicity and accuracy in time-window logic. The next lesson returns to contractual date boundaries and how activities can fall outside a service period.

G07-T12.open: This lesson is about making sure activity stays inside a valid contract window. The important distinction is between proactive expiry monitoring and reactive detection of orders already placed after the contract ended.

questions.q: What boundary does Step 1 actually enforce in the query?
choices: The upper bound, by flagging orders placed after ContractEnd
The lower bound, by flagging orders before ContractStart exactly
A fiscal-year boundary only
A VAT boundary
questions.right: Correct. The query explicitly flags orders after the contract end date.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains that the full rule would check both start and end, but the code shown mainly enforces the upper bound because it only derives a start date for illustration.

questions.q: Why is Step 2 considered proactive compliance monitoring?
choices: Because it surfaces contracts that are about to expire so renewal action can happen before a violation
Because it already proves a violation occurred
Because it only looks at cancelled orders
Because it calculates tax exposure
questions.right: Yes. It is a warning mechanism, not just a retrospective violation report.
questions.wrong: The lesson contrasts proactive monitoring with reactive detection. Step 2 looks ahead to expiring contracts rather than proving that an activity has already gone wrong.

questions.q: What does the explanation say about grace periods?
choices: They must be modelled explicitly, or valid post-expiry activity may be mis-flagged
They should always be ignored
They are the same as contract start dates
They only apply to refunds
questions.right: Right. The lesson says a real implementation must add grace-period logic if the business allows it.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not say grace periods should be ignored. It warns that without a grace-period adjustment, valid activity may be falsely treated as a violation.

G07-T12.close: This lesson is a straightforward date-range control with a strong reminder that operational rules sometimes need grace periods and contract history tables. The next lesson expands the same compliance idea into geography and sanctioned-region screening.

G07-T13.open: This lesson combines country-based operating restrictions with IP-origin checks. The point is that location validation has both a static dimension, like registered country, and a dynamic one, like source IP.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use two geo-validation layers?
choices: Because registered country and transaction IP origin each reveal different risk signals
Because one layer replaces the other
Because country codes and IP addresses are interchangeable
Because the query is only for product shipping
questions.right: Correct. The explanation explicitly distinguishes static registration country from dynamic transaction origin.
questions.wrong: The lesson says both checks are useful, not interchangeable. Country of registration and source IP each capture a different part of the compliance picture.

questions.q: What is the lesson’s purpose in using `PARSENAME` on `SourceIP`?
choices: To extract the first octet from a dotted IPv4 address
To calculate the customer’s age
To split a product code into category parts
To convert a currency code to lowercase
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses `PARSENAME(..., 4)` as a simple way to grab the first IPv4 octet.
questions.wrong: `PARSENAME` is used here for IP parsing, not age, products, or currency manipulation. The lesson even notes that it was originally designed for object names.

questions.q: What does the lesson say SQL can and cannot do for sanctions screening?
choices: SQL can check approved country lists, but full entity-level sanctions screening needs external data integration
SQL can fully replace sanctions lists if the query is long enough
SQL cannot validate any geographic restriction
SQL only works for UK customers
questions.right: Correct. The explanation explicitly limits SQL’s role to country-code checks and says sanctions screening needs external reference data.
questions.wrong: The lesson is careful here: SQL can validate approved-country membership, but it cannot perform full sanctions screening on its own. The limitation is about entity-level matching, not SQL length or geography.

G07-T13.close: The theme here is that geo-compliance is a layered control, not a single field check. The next lesson shifts to forensic pattern detection, looking for round-number bias and threshold structuring.

G07-T14.open: This lesson is about spotting suspicious amount patterns rather than a hard validity failure. The key idea is that repeated round numbers or amounts just below thresholds often indicate structuring or fabricated entries.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call amounts like £249.99 suspicious near a £250 threshold?
choices: They suggest deliberate structuring just below a control threshold
They are always invalid currency values
They prove the transaction was refunded
They only matter if the customer is under 18
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson treats amounts just under a threshold as a classic control-bypass pattern.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not about currency validity or age rules. It is about deliberate threshold avoidance and structuring behaviour.

questions.q: What does `Amount = ROUND(Amount, -2)` test in Step 1?
choices: Whether the amount is an exact multiple of 100
Whether the amount has two decimal places
Whether the amount is negative
Whether the amount is below £250
questions.right: Correct. The explanation says negative precision rounds to hundreds, so equality means the last two digits are zero.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly explains that negative precision in `ROUND` tests roundness at higher magnitudes. It is not a check for decimal places or negative values.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 compare actual first-digit frequency to Benford’s Law?
choices: To detect distributions that deviate from natural numeric patterns and may signal manipulation
To calculate VAT
To find duplicate transactions
To determine customer age
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses Benford’s distribution as a forensic red-flag, not as a tax or identity rule.
questions.wrong: Benford analysis in this lesson is about forensic anomaly detection. It is not used for VAT, duplicate payment detection, or age eligibility.

G07-T14.close: This lesson is a useful reminder that fraud can be visible in distributions, not just in single bad records. The final lesson in this group turns to approval thresholds and how splitting can bypass them.

G07-T15.open: This lesson applies the inactive-record rule to products, customers, and employees. The central idea is that soft-deleted or terminated records should not keep participating in active business processes.

questions.q: What does `IsActive = 0` mean in this lesson’s explanation?
choices: A soft-delete or inactive flag indicating the record should no longer participate in new transactions
A marker that the record must be physically deleted immediately
A sign the record is duplicated
A VAT exemption code
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly calls `IsActive = 0` a soft-delete pattern.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not treat `IsActive = 0` as a hard delete requirement. It means the record remains for history, but should not be used in new activity.

questions.q: Why does Step 3 filter inactive customers to orders with statuses like Pending, Processing, and Shipped?
choices: Because those are open orders that should not exist for inactive customers
Because delivered orders are the only ones that matter
Because inactive customers are allowed to place any order status
Because the query is really checking tax rates
questions.right: Yes. The lesson is focusing on open activity that should be blocked or resolved when the customer is inactive.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s concern is open orders tied to inactive customers. Delivered orders are not the point of that step, and the query is not about tax.

questions.q: What does Step 2 show about terminated employees and sales targets?
choices: Targets should be reassigned or closed, because leaving them open distorts reporting and commission processing
Terminated employees should keep creating new targets
Targets are only a problem if the employee was a manager
No issue exists if the employee is terminated after the target year
questions.right: Exactly. The explanation says open targets for terminated employees create reporting and payment confusion.
