questions.wrong: The lesson says terminated employees should not continue to be active participants in target-setting. The issue is not limited to managers or to the order of year-end events.

G07-T15.close: This lesson is a broad inactive-entity control: if a record is no longer active, related new activity should stop. The last lesson in the set focuses on threshold bypass through aggregation and splitting.

G07-T16.open: This final lesson in the group is about approval threshold bypass, which is a classic control-evasion pattern. The real detection step is aggregating related orders so you can see the commitment that was split into smaller pieces.

questions.q: Why does Step 1 aggregate by customer and month instead of checking each order individually?
choices: Because splitting orders can hide a total commitment that exceeds the approval threshold
Because monthly totals are always the only legal reporting period
Because individual orders are never stored in the database
Because the threshold applies only to cancelled orders
questions.right: Correct. The lesson’s point is that the combined monthly value can cross the threshold even when no single order does.
questions.wrong: The lesson is not claiming monthly is always the legal period; it is using month as a practical grouping to expose splitting. The control problem is exactly that individual checks can miss the aggregate.

questions.q: What condition in the explanation defines the bypass pattern?
choices: `SUM(TotalAmount)` meets the threshold while `MAX(TotalAmount)` stays below it
`MIN(TotalAmount)` is zero
`COUNT(*)` is exactly one
All orders are cancelled
questions.right: Yes. That is the heart of the detection logic the lesson spells out.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not define bypass by a zero minimum, a single row, or cancelled orders. It specifically looks for an aggregate that triggers the threshold without any single record doing so.

questions.q: Why does the lesson include a near-threshold check like 5% below the threshold?
choices: To catch deliberate amounts that are just under approval levels
To identify refunds
To find inactive customers
To measure VAT changes
questions.right: Right. The lesson says this is the single-transaction equivalent of structuring and is suspicious when repeated.
questions.wrong: The near-threshold check is not about refunds, inactivity, or tax. It is there to detect attempts to stay just below an approval boundary.

G07-T16.close: This lesson closes the group with the pattern that underlies several others: validate the aggregate, not just the row. That same idea appears in credit, stock, and velocity checks throughout Group 7.

G08-T01.open: This lesson builds on the reconciliation pattern from Group 8: recompute detail totals, compare them to a stored header, and treat tolerance carefully. Here the twist is that rounding differences and missing detail rows can look similar unless you inspect discrepancy size and line patterns.

questions.q: Why does the query compare `o.TotalAmount` to `ISNULL(dt.DetailSum, 0)` instead of only to `dt.DetailSum`?
choices: So orders with no transactions still appear as mismatches instead of being filtered out by a NULL comparison
So SQL can automatically convert all amounts to integers before summing
So the join becomes faster than an inner join in every case
So `SUM(Amount)` ignores negative values in the Transactions table
questions.right: Exactly. `ISNULL(dt.DetailSum, 0)` lets the query flag header-only orders as reconciliation failures instead of letting NULL hide the problem.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s logic is about preserving unmatched headers, not about type conversion, join speed, or filtering out negative amounts.

questions.q: What does the 0.01 tolerance in the WHERE clause and CASE expression represent in this lesson?
choices: A one-penny tolerance to avoid false positives from tiny rounding differences
A requirement that every discrepancy be exactly one cent
A way to round all results down to the nearest pound
A rule that only orders with at least one transaction should be checked
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly uses a 1-penny tolerance so legitimate rounding noise does not become a false mismatch.
questions.wrong: The lesson treats 0.01 as a tolerance band, not as a mandatory discrepancy size or a row-filtering rule.

questions.q: What is the point of Step 4’s line-count analysis?
choices: To test whether larger discrepancies tend to increase with more line items, which would support cumulative rounding as the cause
To convert the monthly totals into yearly totals
To remove duplicate Orders before comparing headers
To find transactions with negative amounts only
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses line count as evidence: if discrepancy rises with more lines, rounding accumulation is the likely explanation.
questions.wrong: Step 4 is about diagnosing the source of mismatch, not aggregating by year, deduplicating orders, or isolating negatives.

G08-T01.close: That lesson is the classic header-vs-detail reconciliation pattern with a tolerance and a diagnostic drill-down. Next comes a broader count reconciliation across related systems and relationship-level gaps.

G08-T02.open: This one expands reconciliation from single totals to counts and relationship integrity. It stays in the Group 8 pattern but shifts from amount mismatches to missing rows, orphan rows, and ratio checks.

questions.q: Why does Step 2 use `NOT EXISTS` to find orders without transactions?
choices: It efficiently checks whether a matching child row exists without building a full join result
It forces SQL Server to sort the tables before scanning them
It guarantees the order count and transaction count are equal
It only works when the child table has fewer rows than the parent table
questions.right: Correct. The lesson positions `NOT EXISTS` as an efficient existence check for relationship-level reconciliation.
questions.wrong: The lesson is about existence checks, not forced sorting, guaranteeing equality, or relying on relative table sizes.

questions.q: What does Step 3’s transaction-to-order ratio help detect?
choices: Whether the child-row volume is unusually low or high relative to the parent-row count
Whether every order was entered on the same date
Whether transactions were rounded to two decimals
Whether customers have missing phone numbers
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses ratio analysis to spot missing transactions or suspiciously high child-row counts relative to orders.
questions.wrong: The ratio is a reconciliation signal, not a date check, rounding check, or customer-data quality check.

questions.q: What does the CustomerCoveragePct metric measure in Step 5?
choices: The percentage of customers who have at least one order
The percentage of orders that are fully paid
The share of products that were sold in the warehouse
The percentage of transactions that have a null currency
questions.right: Exactly. It compares distinct customers in Orders against total customers in Customers to show coverage.
questions.wrong: The lesson defines it as customer-to-order coverage, not payment status, product movement, or currency completeness.

G08-T02.close: The main idea is that row counts alone are not enough; you also need relationship checks and expected ratios. The next lesson turns from counts to cash reconciliation across two independently maintained records.

G08-T03.open: This lesson moves from simple counts into a formal reconciliation statement. The key idea is not just finding a variance, but separating period totals, unmatched items, and an ending outstanding balance.

questions.q: Why does the monthly reconciliation use a `FULL OUTER JOIN` between MonthlyOrders and MonthlyTransactions?
choices: To keep months that exist on only one side visible in the result
To force duplicate rows to be removed automatically
To convert transaction amounts into order currency
To filter out cancelled orders before aggregation
questions.right: Exactly. A full outer join preserves periods present in only one dataset, which is essential for two-sided reconciliation.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses the join to preserve unmatched periods, not to deduplicate, convert currency, or filter cancellations.

questions.q: What does Step 5’s OutstandingBalance represent?
choices: The remaining unreconciled amount after comparing total order value to settled transaction value
The total number of orders that were cancelled
The average transaction amount per order
The number of months with a non-zero variance
questions.right: Correct. It is the remaining difference between total order value and the amount settled by transactions.
questions.wrong: The lesson defines it as an amount gap, not a count, average, or month tally.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 use amount proximity to identify near matches?
choices: To surface probable transposition or small-value mismatches that should be reviewed manually
To prove that all mismatches are caused by rounding
To exclude every order that already has a transaction
To convert the query into a bank statement report
questions.right: Yes. The lesson treats near matches as investigative leads, especially when a transposition error may be involved.
questions.wrong: The lesson is about review leads, not proof of rounding, exclusion of matched rows, or conversion into a different report type.

G08-T03.close: This lesson formalizes reconciliation as totals, unmatched items, and an outstanding balance that must be explained. Next is the same identity applied to opening balance, movements, and closing balance over time.

G08-T04.open: Here the reconciliation pattern becomes a running-balance check. Instead of comparing one total to another, the lesson validates the period identity: opening plus net movement should land on the next closing balance.

questions.q: What does `SUM(NetMovement) OVER (ORDER BY Yr, Mo ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` calculate in this lesson?
choices: A cumulative running balance across periods
A distinct count of transaction dates
The average monthly debit value
A list of missing months in the sequence
questions.right: Correct. The windowed SUM builds the cumulative balance period by period.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses the window aggregate for running totals, not distinct counts, averages, or gap detection.

questions.q: What is the purpose of `LAG(CumulativeNet) OVER (ORDER BY Yr, Mo)` in Step 2?
choices: To compare the current period’s cumulative balance with the prior period’s cumulative balance
To find the earliest transaction in the month
To remove duplicate months from the result
To convert debits into credits automatically
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses LAG to validate that each period’s movement matches the change from the previous cumulative balance.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses LAG for period-over-period comparison, not deduplication, min-date lookup, or sign conversion.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 convert year and month into `Yr * 12 + Mo`?
choices: To make consecutive periods easy to compare as a single numeric sequence
To sort months alphabetically
To calculate the number of days in each period
To force SQL Server to use decimal arithmetic
questions.right: Exactly. That transformation makes it easy to detect whether there is a gap of more than one period.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses the formula for sequence continuity, not alphabetic ordering, date math, or decimal coercion.

G08-T04.close: The lesson’s core is the accounting identity plus window functions for running validation and gap detection. Next comes a consolidation problem where internal entities must be eliminated rather than merely matched.

G08-T05.open: This lesson shifts from external reconciliation into consolidation. The main challenge is identifying internal entities and then checking that the mirrored intercompany amounts actually cancel out.

questions.q: Why does the query first build an `InternalCustomers` CTE?
choices: To isolate customers flagged as internal entities before matching them to intercompany orders
To convert all currencies to GBP
To count only cancelled orders
To remove orders without a transaction
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly filters internal customers first so later joins focus on intercompany activity.
questions.wrong: The CTE is for entity filtering, not currency conversion, cancellation filtering, or orphan removal.

questions.q: What does `STRING_AGG(t.Currency, ', ')` help reveal in Step 1?
choices: Whether an order was settled in more than one currency, which is a currency-mismatch warning
How many customers are internal entities
The oldest transaction date in the group
Whether the order was cancelled after posting
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses the aggregated currency list to spot multi-currency intercompany pairs and exchange-rate risk.
questions.wrong: The currency list is diagnostic for settlement mismatch, not customer counts, date age, or cancellation logic.

questions.q: What is Step 2 meant to provide beyond individual-order reconciliation?
choices: A roll-up of total intercompany exposure by entity
A list of all products sold to customers
A monthly tax return summary
A check for duplicate payment dates
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson says Step 2 is for the total uneliminated balance per subsidiary or entity.
questions.wrong: Step 2 is an entity exposure rollup, not product, tax, or duplicate-payment analysis.

G08-T05.close: This one is about elimination, not just matching: intercompany balances must vanish in consolidation. The next lesson turns to a different control-account drift problem between a sub-ledger and the GL.

G08-T06.open: The reconciliation theme stays the same, but the accounting structure changes: a detail ledger versus a control total. The lesson emphasizes both monthly variance and cumulative drift so you can tell whether the problem is recurring.

questions.q: What does `CumulativeDrift` in Step 1 measure?
choices: The running sum of monthly differences between the control total and the sub-ledger
The average transaction amount per month
The total number of cancelled orders
The age of the oldest unreconciled invoice
questions.right: Correct. It accumulates the monthly variance over time to show whether the gap is growing.
questions.wrong: The lesson defines drift as a cumulative variance, not an average, cancellation count, or invoice age.

questions.q: Why does the CASE expression distinguish both positive and negative variance directions?
choices: Because control-over-subledger and subledger-over-control point to different posting problems
Because positive variances must always be rounded up
Because negative variances mean transactions are cancelled
Because the query only works for months with exactly one order
questions.right: Yes. The lesson explicitly treats the sign as meaningful: one direction means GL only, the other means sub-ledger only.
questions.wrong: The sign is diagnostic in this lesson; it is not about rounding, cancellation, or one-order months.

questions.q: What is Step 3’s purpose?
choices: To identify specific orders that exist in the control system but have no matching sub-ledger transaction
To calculate VAT on each product
To find customers with no orders
To detect missing periods in a calendar
questions.right: Exactly. It drills from drift totals down to the records that caused the control-only posting.
questions.wrong: Step 3 is a missing-posting drill-down, not a VAT, customer, or calendar analysis.

G08-T06.close: The lesson shows how small monthly variances compound into cumulative drift and where to drill down for specific unposted items. Next is multi-currency reconciliation, where the first mistake is summing unlike amounts at all.

G08-T07.open: This lesson is about a subtle but dangerous error: adding transactions across currencies as if they were interchangeable. The fix starts with breaking totals out by currency, then converting with explicit rates before any combined total is trusted.

questions.q: Why does Step 1 group by `Currency` before summing amounts?
choices: To avoid mixing different currencies into a meaningless total
To automatically convert every amount into GBP
To sort transactions by exchange-rate volatility
To identify cancelled orders
questions.right: Correct. The lesson’s first rule is to separate currencies before any aggregate is interpreted.
questions.wrong: The query does not convert automatically or analyze cancellations; it isolates currencies first.

questions.q: What does Step 2 flag when `CurrencyCount > 1` for an order?
choices: That the order contains multiple currencies and cannot be summed directly without conversion
That the order is guaranteed to be overpaid
That the order was posted before its order date
That the order must be cancelled
questions.right: Yes. The lesson labels this a multi-currency order and warns against direct summation.
questions.wrong: Multiple currencies are a reconciliation warning, not proof of overpayment, cutoff error, or cancellation.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 check for `LEN(Currency) <> 3` and blank values?
choices: Because invalid or missing ISO 4217 codes cannot be converted reliably
Because all valid currencies must be numeric
Because the amount field should be three characters long
Because blank currencies always mean cancelled orders
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson treats malformed currency codes as a pre-conversion data quality issue.
questions.wrong: The lesson is validating currency codes, not numeric formats, amount length, or cancellation status.

G08-T07.close: The core warning is simple: raw sums across currencies are deceptive unless you know the mix and the conversion basis. The next lesson moves from currency mix-ups to period cutoff errors around the order date and posting date.

G08-T08.open: This lesson focuses on timing: the economic date of the order versus the date the transaction was posted. The main idea is that a valid amount can still be wrong if it lands in the wrong accounting period.

questions.q: What does the lesson treat as the cutoff problem?
choices: A transaction recorded in a different year-month from the related order
A transaction with too many decimal places
A customer with no email address
An order with more than one product
questions.right: Correct. The lesson defines cutoff errors as period mismatches between the economic activity date and the posting date.
questions.wrong: The lesson is about period timing, not decimal precision, customer attributes, or product counts.

questions.q: Why does Step 3 flag transactions near month-end using `DAY(EOMONTH(TransactionDate)) - DAY(TransactionDate)`?
choices: Because transactions close to month-end are at the highest risk of slipping into the next period
Because those transactions always have zero value
Because month-end records must be cancelled
Because `EOMONTH` converts amounts to integers
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses proximity to month-end as a practical risk indicator for cutoff issues.
questions.wrong: The query is about period risk, not zero values, cancellations, or numeric type conversion.

questions.q: What does the direction in Step 2 tell you?
choices: Whether revenue was recognized too early or too late, which changes the needed adjustment entry
Whether the customer is internal or external
Whether the order amount is taxable
Whether the transaction uses GBP or USD
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson uses direction to decide whether to reverse the current period or adjust a prior period.
questions.wrong: Direction here is about timing adjustment, not entity type, tax, or currency.

G08-T08.close: The lesson is all about period boundaries and whether revenue landed where it belongs. Next is duplicate payment detection, where the focus shifts from timing to repeated cash outflow.

G08-T09.open: This lesson is about identifying when the same invoice was paid more than once. It separates exact duplicates from near-duplicates and also distinguishes legitimate split payments from true overpayments.

questions.q: Why does the exact-duplicate query group by `OrderID, Amount, Currency` and use `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`?
choices: To find repeated payments for the same invoice amount and currency
To find every order with exactly one payment
To convert duplicate rows into unique rows automatically
To identify transactions older than 30 days
questions.right: Correct. That grouping key is the core duplicate-detection pattern described in the lesson.
questions.wrong: The lesson is looking for repeated payments, not single-payment orders, automatic deduplication, or age filtering.

questions.q: What does the self-join condition `t1.TransactionID < t2.TransactionID` accomplish in Step 2?
choices: It prevents mirrored duplicate pairs from appearing twice
It ensures only cancelled transactions are included
It forces the join to match different currencies only
It rounds both transaction dates to the nearest month
questions.right: Yes. The lesson explains that this avoids showing both A-B and B-A for the same near-duplicate pair.
questions.wrong: The condition is about pair deduplication, not cancellation, currency separation, or date rounding.

questions.q: How does Step 3 distinguish split payments from overpayments?
choices: Two transactions that sum exactly to the order total are treated as split payments; sums above the total are overpaid
Any order with two transactions is always a duplicate
Any order with one transaction is always an overpayment
Split payments are defined by negative amounts only
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson explicitly says not all multi-transaction orders are duplicates; the total versus order value determines the status.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses amount-sum logic, not transaction count alone or negative-only rules.

G08-T09.close: The lesson’s key lesson is that duplicate detection needs both grouping and judgement about legitimate split payments. Next comes fan-out double-counting, where the error is not extra cash but an inflated aggregate from a bad join.

G08-T10.open: This lesson tackles a classic analytics mistake: joining a one-row-per-order table to a multi-row-per-order table, then summing the header value after the join. The result is not a data-quality issue in the source so much as a granularity error in the query.

questions.q: What causes the fan-out error in this lesson?
choices: Summing `Orders.TotalAmount` after a one-to-many join to Transactions
Using `GROUP BY` on the Orders table
Filtering cancelled orders before aggregation
Selecting only distinct TransactionID values
questions.right: Correct. The lesson’s central warning is that the header row gets repeated once per matching transaction.
questions.wrong: The other choices are not the cause of fan-out; the issue is aggregate placement after the join.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend aggregating transactions first into a CTE?
choices: So each order joins to exactly one transaction total, preventing header multiplication
So duplicate orders are removed from the database
So all monthly totals become yearly totals
So `SUM(DISTINCT)` can be avoided by converting amounts to strings
questions.right: Yes. The aggregate-first pattern collapses the many-side to one row per order before joining.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses the CTE to control join granularity, not to delete orders, change time scale, or stringify amounts.

questions.q: What does `COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT o.OrderID)` tell you in Step 2?
choices: How many extra rows were created by fan-out
How many orders were cancelled
How many currencies appear in the dataset
How many orders have no transactions
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson uses that difference as the diagnostic count of multiplied join rows.
questions.wrong: The metric measures extra join rows, not cancellations, currency variety, or missing children.

G08-T10.close: The whole point is to keep aggregation aligned with grain. Next is unallocated cash, where the problem is a payment that exists but cannot be matched to any invoice at all.

G08-T11.open: This lesson is about cash that arrived but has no valid invoice or order linkage. The focus is on orphan transactions, ageing them, and then looking for plausible matches without pretending the match is certain.

questions.q: What does `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = t.OrderID)` detect in Step 1?
choices: Transactions with no valid parent order, including NULL and invalid OrderID values
Only transactions older than 90 days
Only orders that were cancelled
Only duplicate transactions with the same amount
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly says it catches both NULL references and non-existent OrderIDs.
questions.wrong: The check is about orphaned transactions, not age thresholds, cancellation, or duplicate amounts.

questions.q: Why does Step 2 group unallocated cash by age band?
choices: To prioritize older unresolved receipts because they are harder to resolve
To convert all amounts to the oldest transaction date
To find products with zero stock
To prove the payment was duplicated
questions.right: Yes. The lesson says age bands help the AR team prioritize fresh items first and escalate stale ones later.
questions.wrong: Age bands are about triage, not conversion, inventory, or proving duplication.

questions.q: What is Step 3 trying to do with amount and date proximity?
choices: Suggest likely matches for unallocated receipts that the AR team can manually confirm
Delete unmatched receipts from the ledger
Mark every near match as definitively reconciled
Convert foreign currency receipts into GBP automatically
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson frames Step 3 as fuzzy matching for investigation, not automatic posting.
questions.wrong: The query is advisory, not destructive, not definitive, and not a currency conversion routine.

G08-T11.close: This lesson treats unmatched cash as a triage problem: find the orphans, bucket them by age, and suggest likely allocations. The next lesson turns to stock counts versus system balance.

G08-T12.open: This lesson reuses the reconciliation pattern for inventory. Instead of invoices and cash, it compares the system’s book balance to physical stock signals and flags products whose movement pattern does not make sense.

questions.q: What does the lesson use as a proxy for inventory movement when no dedicated stock movement table exists?
choices: The Orders table, where each order is treated as an outbound movement signal
The Customers table, where each customer is one unit of stock
The Transactions table only when amounts are negative
The Products table price field
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says Orders provide a proxy for movement when a dedicated movement table is absent.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not use customers as stock units, negative transactions only, or product prices as movement records.

questions.q: Why does the query flag `StockQuantity = 0 AND COUNT(o.OrderID) > 0`?
choices: Because orders exist despite zero stock, suggesting oversell, count error, or a missed receipt
Because zero stock means the product must be inactive
Because every zero-stock product is fully reconciled
Because the product has no VAT rate
questions.right: Yes. The lesson treats that combination as a classic stock discrepancy signal requiring investigation.
questions.wrong: Zero stock is not automatically benign or tied to VAT; the issue is sales activity against an empty balance.

questions.q: What is Step 3 measuring with `UnsettledOrders` and `OutstandingBalance`?
choices: How much order value remains unmatched by transaction value for each product
How many products are marked inactive
How many refunds were issued in the current month
How many customers live in each country
questions.right: Exactly. It’s the product-level settlement gap, not an inactivity or geography report.
questions.wrong: The lesson uses product-level outstanding value, not product status counts, refund volume, or customer geography.

G08-T12.close: The lesson’s theme is that physical or system stock inconsistencies often show up first as mismatched movement patterns. Next is tax reconciliation, where the same compare-and-flag logic is applied to VAT.

G08-T13.open: This lesson applies reconciliation to tax: derive the VAT component from gross order values, then compare the computed tax with what was actually collected. It also emphasizes that only valid VAT rates should be in play.

questions.q: How does the lesson derive VAT from a VAT-inclusive gross amount?
choices: By computing net as `Gross / (1 + Rate/100)` and then VAT as `Gross - Net`
By multiplying gross by the rate directly
By subtracting the rate percentage from the gross amount
By dividing gross by the number of transactions
questions.right: Correct. That is the formula described in the explanation and used in the query.
questions.wrong: The lesson explicitly uses the reverse-calculation formula, not direct multiplication or unrelated arithmetic.

questions.q: Why does Step 3 flag VAT rates not in `(0, 5, 20)`?
choices: Because those are the valid UK VAT rates the lesson expects
Because every rate above 20 is automatically tax-free
Because only 0% and 20% are ever legal in the UK
Because VAT rates must be stored as text
questions.right: Yes. The lesson names 0%, 5%, and 20% as the valid UK rate set for this exercise.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s own framing allows 0%, 5%, and 20%, not just two rates or text storage.

questions.q: What does Step 4 compare?
choices: VAT computed from invoice data against total transaction amounts received
Customer age bands against product prices
Stock quantities against order counts
Transaction counts against supplier names
questions.right: Exactly. It is the tax-control-account-style reconciliation at the end of the lesson.
questions.wrong: The lesson’s final comparison is tax versus receipts, not ageing, stock, or supplier-name checks.

G08-T13.close: The lesson is a tax version of the broader reconciliation pattern: compute expected tax, compare it to actuals, and watch for rate mistakes. Next is the aged debtor report, where outstanding balances are bucketed by age and checked against expected customer totals.

G08-T14.open: This lesson combines reconciliation with receivables ageing. It first computes invoice-level outstanding balances, then rolls them up into customer and portfolio age bands, and finally checks for overpaid customers.

questions.q: Why does the CTE in Step 1 use `HAVING o.TotalAmount - ISNULL(SUM(t.Amount), 0) > 0.01`?
choices: To keep only invoices that still have a meaningful outstanding balance
To include only cancelled orders
To round every invoice to the nearest whole pound
To sort customers alphabetically
questions.right: Correct. The lesson uses HAVING to filter out settled orders after aggregation.
questions.wrong: The filter is about outstanding balance, not cancellation, whole-pound rounding, or sorting.

questions.q: What do the age-band SUM expressions in Step 1 do?
choices: They pivot outstanding balances into separate customer aging columns
They convert overdue invoices into credits
They remove customers with zero orders
They calculate VAT on receivables
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses conditional SUM to create the standard AR aging breakdown in one row per customer.
questions.wrong: The expressions are for aging buckets, not credit conversion, row removal, or tax calculation.

questions.q: What does Step 3’s negative `ImpliedOutstanding` indicate?
choices: The customer has paid more than invoiced, which may indicate duplicate payment or misallocation
The customer has no orders
The customer is on a 90+ day aging bucket
The ledger is perfectly reconciled
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson states that overpayment creates a liability and may indicate a duplicate or wrong-customer allocation.
questions.wrong: Negative outstanding is not the same as no orders, age banding, or a clean reconciliation.

G08-T14.close: The lesson’s structure mirrors a real AR aging workflow: build invoice balances, classify them by age, then identify overpayment anomalies. The final lesson is a batch control-total check, where completeness matters more than tolerance.

G08-T15.open: This lesson is the batch-file version of reconciliation. Rather than comparing business balances, it verifies that declared control totals match the actual record count and total amount, with zero tolerance for mismatch.

questions.q: Why does Step 1 use `@Tolerance = 0.00`?
choices: Because batch control totals must match exactly, not within a rounding band
Because decimals are not allowed in Transactions
Because only negative amounts are valid in batch files
Because `CHECKSUM_AGG` can only work with zero tolerance
questions.right: Correct. The lesson contrasts batch-file control totals with business-data tolerances and says batch files need exact matches.
questions.wrong: The zero tolerance is about exact control-total verification, not decimal rules, sign rules, or checksum limitations.

questions.q: What does `CHECKSUM_AGG(CHECKSUM(...))` provide in this lesson?
choices: A compact integrity value that changes if records are altered after the batch load
A count of cancelled orders
A guarantee that no rows were rejected
A replacement for monthly aging analysis
questions.right: Yes. The lesson uses it as a batch-state fingerprint for post-load verification.
questions.wrong: The checksum is for change detection, not cancellation counts, rejection proof, or aging.

questions.q: What does the sequence gap query detect?
choices: Missing TransactionID values that suggest lost, rejected, or never-loaded records
Orders that have no products
Customers with duplicate names
Currency codes that are not three letters long
questions.right: Exactly. The lesson explains that a gap in sequential IDs can indicate missing records in the batch.
questions.wrong: The gap check is about missing IDs, not order composition, customer names, or currency format.

G08-T15.close: The lesson’s message is that control totals and sequence checks are completeness controls, not business-rule checks. That completes the reconciliation group: from header-detail mismatches through batch verification and every major reconciliation pattern in between.

G09-T01.open: This lesson starts the Timeliness group by treating staleness as an age test against the current date. Keep that same comparison pattern in mind, because later lessons in this group reuse it for latency, expiry, and reporting freshness.

questions.q: Why does the main stale-order check filter out Delivered, Cancelled, and Refunded statuses before applying the 30-day age threshold?
choices: Because terminal states are complete records and are not expected to change further
Because GETDATE() cannot be used on terminal records
Because those statuses always indicate future-dated orders
Because only refunded orders can be older than 30 days
questions.right: Correct. The lesson treats those statuses as terminal, so stale monitoring should only apply where more processing is still expected.
questions.wrong: The query excludes terminal states because they are already complete. The age threshold is meant for open work, not records that should never progress again.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the delivery-date check in Step 3?
choices: To find orders where the promised delivery date has passed but the status is still not Delivered
To find orders that were cancelled before they shipped
To calculate the average shipping cost per customer
To identify orders whose delivery date is exactly 30 days after the order date
questions.right: Correct. Step 3 is specifically about orders whose promised delivery date is already in the past while the status remains non-terminal.
questions.wrong: Step 3 is not about cancellations or cost analysis. It targets overdue deliveries where the system still has not marked the order as Delivered.

questions.q: Why does the explanation say the threshold should be parameterised for different domains?
choices: Because the right freshness window depends on the workflow, such as 24 hours for clinical records or 1 minute for trading data
Because SQL Server only supports one hardcoded threshold per database
Because all data quality checks must use 30 days by law
Because GETDATE() only works with parameters
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly says timeliness thresholds vary by domain and should be adjusted to the workflow being monitored.
questions.wrong: The lesson gives different examples to show that freshness windows are business-driven, not fixed at 30 days for every system.

G09-T01.close: You have the core stale-data pattern now: compare record age to a threshold, then separate open work from terminal states. The next timeliness lessons build the same idea into latency, SLA, and expiry checks.

G09-T02.open: This lesson extends the timeliness theme from age into lag: not just whether data is old, but whether it arrived late relative to an SLA. The key reasoning is to measure the gap between two timestamps and then classify the size of that gap.

questions.q: Why does Step 1 use DATEDIFF(HOUR, o.OrderDate, t.TransactionDate) instead of DATEDIFF(DAY, ... ) for the SLA check?
choices: Because the SLA is about hour-level latency, so hour precision is the better fit
Because DATEDIFF(DAY) cannot be used with dates
Because hour differences always return decimal values
Because day differences are only valid for future dates
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says the SLA is easier to express in hours or minutes, and Step 1 uses hours to measure arrival lag.
questions.wrong: The query can use day differences, but that would be too coarse for a latency SLA. The lesson explicitly prefers a unit that matches the SLA definition.

questions.q: What does a negative LagHours value mean in this lesson's logic?
choices: The transaction timestamp is earlier than the order timestamp, which is treated as a data integrity error
The order is delayed by exactly one day
The transaction was successfully delivered early
The order has already been cancelled
questions.right: Correct. A negative lag means the timestamps are in the wrong order, which the lesson treats as an impossible sequence unless there is a time-zone or backdating issue.
questions.wrong: Negative lag is not an on-time or cancelled state. It signals that the transaction appears to predate the order, which is an integrity problem.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 treat orders with no transaction as a latency issue?
choices: Because a record that never arrives has effectively infinite latency, so absence itself is a breach condition
Because missing transactions are automatically marked as cancelled
Because GETDATE() returns NULL for missing records
Because only late transactions matter, not missing ones
questions.right: Correct. The lesson frames a never-arriving record as the extreme case of latency, and Step 4 measures how long it has been absent.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not ignore missing records. It treats them as the strongest possible latency problem because the data never showed up at all.

G09-T02.close: The important idea here is that lateness can be measured, banded, and reported just like staleness. Next lessons in the group keep reusing that same timestamp comparison pattern in different failure modes.

G09-T03.open: This lesson moves from arrival lag to processing-time SLA breaches, which is a different but related timing problem. Instead of asking whether data came late, it asks how long an item stayed open before reaching a terminal state.

questions.q: In Step 1, what does ProcessingDays represent for delivered orders?
choices: The number of calendar days between OrderDate and DeliveryDate
The number of business days excluding weekends
The number of hours between order and delivery
The number of days since the last customer login
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly uses DATEDIFF(DAY, OrderDate, DeliveryDate), which counts calendar days.
questions.wrong: The query does not calculate business days or hours. The explanation calls out that this is a calendar-day calculation and that business-day SLAs need a different approach.

questions.q: Why does the explanation say a calendar-table approach may be needed for business-day SLAs?
choices: Because DATEDIFF(DAY) counts weekends too, while a business-day SLA should exclude them
Because calendar tables are the only way to join Orders and Customers
Because DATEDIFF(DAY) cannot compare two dates
Because business-day SLAs are always less than 24 hours
questions.right: Correct. The lesson points out that calendar days include weekends, so business-day calculations need a more detailed date structure.
questions.wrong: The issue is not joining tables or date comparison ability. The issue is that simple day differences include weekends, which is not what a business-day SLA means.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the percentile query in Step 4?
choices: To understand the spread of processing times so SLA targets can be set from historical distribution, not just the mean
To calculate the exact delivery cost for each order
To convert delivered orders into pending orders
To identify customers who have never ordered
questions.right: Correct. The lesson uses percentiles to show how historical performance can guide achievable SLA targets.
questions.wrong: Step 4 is about the distribution of delivery times, not costs or customer onboarding. The lesson specifically uses median and upper percentiles to inform SLA design.

G09-T03.close: Processing-time checks are about how long work stays unresolved, not just whether it is old. The next lessons reuse date arithmetic again, but with future dates, backdating, and other sequence errors.

G09-T04.open: This lesson starts the date-anomaly side of timeliness: records that point into the future when they should not. The main pattern is still simple comparison, but the lesson adds tolerance bands so scheduled records are not confused with genuine errors.

questions.q: Why does the query use CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE) when checking for future-dated values?
choices: To strip the time portion and avoid treating a record from earlier today as future-dated because of clock time
To make all future dates round up to the nearest month
To convert local time into UTC automatically
To force all records into the year 2099
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explains that stripping the time avoids edge cases where today’s date could be misread because of time-of-day comparisons.
questions.wrong: The cast is not about timezone conversion or artificial year changes. It simply removes the time component so the comparison is date-based.

questions.q: What is the lesson's purpose for checking YEAR(ContractEnd) > 2090?
choices: To catch a pattern typical of 2-digit year migration errors that become 2090-2099
To identify all perpetual contracts as invalid
To detect contracts that expire next month
To prove the customer has cancelled
questions.right: Correct. The explanation ties 2090+ dates to a common migration bug where 1990s values were shifted into the 2090s.
questions.wrong: The query is not flagging normal short-term expiries or cancellations. It is looking for the specific signature of a year-conversion problem.

questions.q: Why are future dates not always treated as errors in this lesson?
choices: Because some systems legitimately schedule orders or contracts in advance, so the query uses tolerance windows to separate expected from suspicious values
Because GETDATE() cannot detect future dates reliably
Because all future values are automatically business as usual
Because ContractEnd must always be at least 10 years ahead
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly says scheduled future events can be legitimate, so the logic uses day and year thresholds to classify risk.
questions.wrong: Future dates are not accepted blindly. The lesson distinguishes planned future dates from likely data-entry or migration errors using threshold bands.

G09-T04.close: The future-date pattern is now in place: compare to today, then apply a tolerance instead of assuming every future value is wrong. Next comes the opposite problem, where a record claims to belong to the past before it was actually created.

G09-T05.open: This lesson flips the date-error direction and looks for backdating. The core idea is to compare the business date to a more trustworthy sequence and look for impossible or suspicious timing patterns.

questions.q: Why is t.TransactionDate < o.OrderDate considered impossible in the lesson's explanation?
choices: Because a payment for an order should not be recorded before the order exists
Because transactions always happen after delivery, not after ordering
Because orders cannot have a customer attached
Because DATEDIFF only works for same-day records
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says the transaction is triggered by the order existing, so a transaction before the order indicates backdating or a data error.
questions.wrong: The issue is not delivery timing or customer linkage. It is the impossible sequence of recording the related transaction before the parent order date.

questions.q: What does Step 2's month-end clustering try to detect?
choices: A suspicious concentration of orders on the last day of a month, which can indicate revenue manipulation or backdating
Customers who placed orders at midnight
Orders that have no customer records
Transactions with negative amounts
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says a spike on the last day of the month or quarter is a classic backdating signal that should be audited.
questions.wrong: The query is not about midnight timing or negative amounts. It looks for abnormal clustering at period end, which can support a backdating investigation.

questions.q: Why does the explanation say audit log timestamps are more reliable than the business date?
choices: Because users can usually edit the business date, but not the system-assigned creation timestamp
Because audit logs are always older than the business date
Because business dates are never used in reporting
Because order dates and audit timestamps are the same thing
questions.right: Correct. The lesson makes the audit timestamp the more trustworthy control because it is system-assigned and not user-editable.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not treat audit logs as older business dates or the same thing as order dates. It relies on the audit timestamp as a tamper-resistant reference point.

G09-T05.close: The takeaway is that backdating is often a sequence problem, not just a date problem. The next timeliness lesson shifts to missing batches and load monitoring, where absence of data is itself the issue.

G09-T06.open: This lesson turns from record-level timing problems to batch-level monitoring. The idea is to compare today's data volume to historical norms and to detect whole missing days, not just late individual records.

questions.q: Why does Step 1 compare each day's count to the average of the previous seven days rather than the current day's overall average?
choices: Because a trailing average gives a realistic expected baseline without using the current day itself in the comparison
Because the current day count must always be included in its own average
Because rolling averages only work for amounts, not counts
Because historical averages cannot be used in SQL Server
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says the trailing seven-day average is the expected baseline and excludes the current day from the calculation.
questions.wrong: The query intentionally excludes the current day so the baseline is not distorted by the value being tested. That is the point of the trailing window.

questions.q: What is the main reason a day with DailyCount = 0 is treated differently from a low-volume day?
choices: A zero-record day suggests the batch did not run or produced nothing, which is stronger evidence of a missing load than natural volume fluctuation
A zero-record day is always normal on weekends
A zero-record day means the data was archived successfully
A zero-record day only matters if amounts are negative
questions.right: Correct. The lesson treats zero records as the strongest signal because it suggests a batch failure, not just unusually low traffic.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not assume zero is normal or archival. It treats zero as a likely batch failure and therefore a high-priority incident.

questions.q: What does the LAG-based gap check add that the rolling average does not?
choices: It identifies missing days in the sequence entirely, which volume checks alone cannot prove
It computes business-day percentages
It replaces the need for TransactionDate
It converts month-level data into customer-level data
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explains that the gap check finds actual missing dates between populated dates, which is different from spotting low counts.
questions.wrong: The LAG check is about missing dates, not business-day math or dimensional reshaping. It complements the volume check by finding holes in the sequence.

G09-T06.close: This lesson shows that batch monitoring needs both volume checks and sequence checks. Next, the group keeps building completeness logic, but now the focus shifts to sequence and ordering across events.

G09-T07.open: This lesson is about order in time, not just the presence of data. It uses sequence checks to catch impossible event ordering, then expands that idea to duplicate storms and payment-before-order cases.

questions.q: What does the LAG function help detect in Step 2?
choices: Whether each transaction happened after the previous transaction for the same order
Whether the order has a customer name
Whether the total amount is positive
Whether the delivery address is missing
questions.right: Correct. The query uses LAG to compare each event against the prior event in the same order sequence.
questions.wrong: LAG is used for chronological comparison within an order. It is not about customer fields or amount sign by itself.

questions.q: Why does Step 4 group by hour and minute of TransactionDate?
choices: To detect multiple transactions landing in the same minute, which can signal retries, replay attacks, or race conditions
To calculate how many customers placed orders in each month
To convert timestamps into UTC
To find refunds that happened on weekends
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly says same-minute clustering can reveal replay or retry storms.
questions.wrong: The grouping is not for timezone conversion or monthly analysis. It is meant to surface event storms where several transactions occur in the same minute.

questions.q: What is the canonical sequence violation highlighted in Step 1?
choices: Delivery before order
Transaction after payment
Customer before country
Order after invoice
questions.right: Correct. The lesson calls delivery before order the clearest impossible sequence.
questions.wrong: The query is not about invoice order or customer geography. The canonical violation in the lesson is that an item cannot be delivered before it was ordered.

G09-T07.close: You now have the sequence-oriented timeliness checks that catch impossible event orderings. The next lesson uses the same date comparisons to monitor expiry and active records that should have lapsed already.

G09-T08.open: This lesson applies timeliness to contract validity rather than event timing. The key pattern is to compare a contract end date to today and then separate expired-active records from those nearing renewal.

questions.q: Why does Step 1 use CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE) when checking whether a contract has expired?
choices: To avoid treating a contract as expired earlier on the same day because of the current time component
To move all contracts to midnight UTC
To make expired contracts reappear as active
To compare against the customer's timezone
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says using the date-only value prevents a contract ending today from being misclassified as expired before the day is over.
questions.wrong: The cast is not about UTC or reactivating contracts. It just removes the time component so the comparison is aligned to whole days.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 30/60/90-day logic in Step 2?
choices: To create a renewal pipeline with urgency bands from operational to strategic planning
To allow contracts to last 90 more days automatically
To reject any contract that expires in less than 90 years
To calculate invoice tax rates
questions.right: Correct. The lesson frames the windows as action bands: urgent, action, and pipeline planning.
questions.wrong: The windows do not extend the contract automatically or change tax. They are used to prioritise renewal work by proximity to expiry.

questions.q: Why are orders placed after ContractEnd considered a violation in Step 3?
choices: Because they indicate post-expiry usage, which can mean revenue leakage and legal risk
Because orders must always be cancelled after expiry
Because contract dates are never relevant to orders
Because DATEDIFF only works for active customers
questions.right: Correct. The lesson links post-expiry orders to unpaid usage and the possibility of deemed renewal by conduct.
questions.wrong: The lesson does not say all post-expiry orders are cancelled or irrelevant. It treats them as evidence that a customer continued using the service after the agreement ended.

G09-T08.close: Expiry monitoring is just another form of timeliness monitoring, but the consequence here is legal and commercial rather than operational. The next lesson pulls freshness into reporting, where the issue is how stale the visible report is compared with source data.

G09-T09.open: This lesson moves from operational freshness to reporting lag. The main concern is whether the most recent data in the source is close enough to today for the report to be trusted.

questions.q: What does MAX(TransactionDate) measure in Step 1?
choices: The most recent source timestamp, which is used as the freshness indicator for the report
The earliest transaction in the table
The number of orders per customer
The average lag between shipments
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says the most recent timestamp shows how far behind the report is.
questions.wrong: MAX(TransactionDate) is not the earliest value or an average. It is the latest source date and therefore the freshness anchor for the report.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the lag threshold is a business requirement rather than a technical constant?
choices: Because different reports tolerate different staleness windows, from minutes for dashboards to days for weekly reports
Because SQL Server decides the threshold automatically
Because all reports must use a 1-day lag
Because transaction tables cannot be checked for freshness
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly says a real-time dashboard and a weekly report do not share the same freshness requirement.
questions.wrong: The threshold is not automatic or universal. The lesson makes it clear that acceptable lag depends on the report's business purpose.

questions.q: What does Step 2's per-order freshness check focus on?
choices: How long it has been since the last transaction for each order, especially for non-terminal orders
Which orders have the highest total amount
Whether every order has a customer with the same name
How many months each order spans
questions.right: Correct. The query uses the last event date per order to see whether an active order has gone quiet for too long.
questions.wrong: Step 2 is not an amount or naming analysis. It checks whether the latest event for an order is stale, especially when the order is still non-terminal.

G09-T09.close: Reporting lag is now tied to a freshness SLA rather than just record age. The last two lessons round out timeliness with retention and completeness, where the question becomes whether data should still exist and whether every period is present.

G09-T10.open: This lesson treats timeliness as a retention problem: data can be too old to keep. The important pattern is comparing last activity or transaction age against a retention period and dealing carefully with NULL dates.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call NULL LastOrderDate a hidden retention failure?
choices: Because NULL values can slip past a cutoff filter and never get selected for deletion
Because NULL means the customer must be active
Because NULL dates are always newer than real dates
Because NULL only appears in financial records
questions.right: Correct. The explanation says a simple less-than cutoff misses NULLs, so those records are retained indefinitely.
questions.wrong: NULL does not mean active or newer. The problem is that NULLs are excluded by ordinary comparison predicates, which can hide old records from deletion logic.

questions.q: What is the difference between the two retention thresholds in the lesson?
choices: One is for customer inactivity retention and the other is for financial record retention, so they have different legal/business meanings
One is for orders and the other for deliveries
One is for future dates and one is for past dates
There is no difference; both mean the same thing
questions.right: Correct. The lesson separates GDPR-style customer retention from financial record retention, which has a different requirement.
questions.wrong: The thresholds are not duplicates. They reflect two separate retention obligations with different purposes and durations.

questions.q: Why does the explanation recommend DATEADD or a day-based comparison for precise retention checks?
choices: Because DATEDIFF(YEAR) is only a rough approximation and can say a year has passed before 365 exact days have elapsed
Because DATEADD is the only function that can handle customers
Because DATEDIFF(YEAR) returns months instead of years
Because day-based comparisons cannot be used in SQL Server
questions.right: Correct. The lesson explicitly warns that DATEDIFF(YEAR) is conservative and can overstate elapsed years near the boundary.
questions.wrong: The issue is not function support. It is precision: year-based differences can move to the next year before the full day count has truly elapsed.

G09-T10.close: Retention logic is different from the other timeliness checks because the goal is deletion or anonymisation, not just detection. The final lesson in the group closes with completeness, where the focus is on making sure every expected period exists.

G09-T11.open: This final Timeliness lesson is about completeness over time: not just whether records are current, but whether every expected month and day exists. It combines period generation, left joins, and gap detection to show where coverage breaks down.

questions.q: Why does Step 1 generate ExpectedMonths instead of only grouping actual transactions by month?
choices: Because completeness checks need the expected periods so missing months can be detected by absence, not just by counts
Because SQL cannot group by month directly
Because transaction dates are not available in the table
Because all months must always have the same count
questions.right: Correct. The lesson emphasizes generating what should exist and then left-joining to what does exist so missing periods become visible.
questions.wrong: The point is not a SQL limitation. It is that completeness requires an expected timeline, otherwise missing months cannot be identified.

questions.q: What does the left join in Step 1 reveal when am.ActYr is NULL?
choices: The expected month has no actual transaction data, so it is a missing period
The month has too many transactions
The month is always a weekend
The month is invalid because the year is missing
questions.right: Correct. A NULL match means the expected month had no actual rows and is therefore a gap.
questions.wrong: NULL here means no matching actual month, not a malformed year or volume spike. It is the signature of a missing period.

questions.q: What is the tradeoff of the LAG-based daily gap detection in Step 2?
choices: It is simpler than building a calendar table, but it cannot tell expected weekend gaps from missed batches without business-day context
It can only detect future dates, not past dates
It always requires a calendar table
It duplicates the monthly completeness check exactly
questions.right: Correct. The lesson says LAG finds adjacent gaps, but a business-day calendar is needed to distinguish legitimate gaps from missing data.
questions.wrong: The LAG approach is deliberately simpler, not dependent on a calendar table. Its limitation is interpretability, not functionality.

G09-T11.close: This completes the completeness side of timeliness: generating expected periods, comparing them to reality, and flagging holes in the timeline. Together with the earlier lessons, you now have the full operational toolkit for stale data, lag, expiry, and missing coverage.
